More UEDEV plugins and resources: uedevlabs.github.io . Want to try it before buying? The free playable demo is a standalone Windows build of the demo levels, and buyers get 57 demo levels free from inside the editor (LCM Nav3D menu > Get the Demo Levels). You can also read everything here as a PDF: the full manual and the quick start . What it does LCM Nav3D is a 3D navigation plugin for Unreal Engine. It builds a sparse voxel octree of the empty space in your level and finds paths through it, so flying and swimming agents can go anywhere there is room for them. You get the full C++ source and every feature is available in Blueprint. Here is what is in it: Area Details GPU builds Voxelization, the octree and its links are built on the GPU (D3D12, D3D11, Vulkan). Each machine tests its GPU's voxels first. If the GPU fails that test, the plugin voxelizes on the CPU for the rest of the session. A GPU path solver is still experimental and will come in a later free update Per-agent cost areas Mark storms, preferred lanes, toll gates and no-fly zones with volumes and the stock NavArea classes. All the planners take them into account, and a stock Navigation Query Filter lets two agents treat the same volume differently. See Cost areas Crowds 10,000+ agents through Mass Entity, with LOD-culled rendering. For comparison, an actor-based AI agent with a controller, movement component and behaviour tree costs about 50 µs per tick Async pathfinding Path requests run off the game thread and call you back when they finish Frame budget Budget settings for the per-frame work. Dynamic-obstacle updates are batched into one window ( r.LcmNav.DynObs.CoalesceMs , 33 ms by default) so the octree is not rebuilt on every single change Memory The octree is sparse. Memory depends on how much geometry your level has, and open sky takes up very little Determinism The same input gives the same path. Replays, lockstep multiplayer and automated tests all depend on that Large worlds World Partition and streaming are supported. You can bake navigation, and a coarse skeleton handles long-range routes before the detailed chunks have loaded Debugging A health check lists anything that would stop agents moving. An auto-tuner tries voxel settings on your own routes and ranks them. There is also a Gameplay Debugger category (about 10 µs) It runs on Unreal Engine 5.2 to 5.8 , on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS, PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S. Each feature above has its own chapter. If you are new, start with Core Concepts . If you are not sure you need 3D navigation at all, read Nav3D vs Recast first. d: LCM Nav3D 3.6.0 release notes (UE 5.2 to 5.8): Fly To predicts moving obstacles, a new Obstacle Gauntlet demo, and GPU voxelization that checks itself.
b: Documentation / Getting Started / What's New in 3.6 What's new in LCM Nav3D 3.6.0 Applies to LCM Nav3D 3.6.0 · Unreal Engine 5.2 to 5.8 · Updated 22 November 2026 Release 3.6.0 (October 2026) supports Unreal Engine 5.2 to 5.8 . Each engine version has its own build of the plugin, so install the one that matches your project. This release adds moving-obstacle prediction to Fly To, a self-check for GPU voxelization, better fish swimming and schooling, and a new Obstacle Gauntlet demo. It also has more than thirty bug fixes from a review of the whole plugin. New Fly To avoids moving obstacles. Fly To now predicts where each moving obstacle (any actor with an LCM Dynamic Obstacle component) will be, and times its pass. It learns the cycle of a gate or a piston, turns with a spinning blade, and slows down, waits for a gap or takes a detour. If something comes at it too fast, it dodges. It is on by default ( Avoid Moving Obstacles , with Moving Obstacle Look-Ahead and Moving Obstacle Margin ) in the Behavior Tree and StateTree Fly To. See Dynamic obstacles . Obstacle Gauntlet demo. A 370 m hall with six zones: fast gates, crossing traffic, windmills and sweepers, pistons, head-on blocks and bouncers. It has 42 moving obstacles, all driven by Unreal's own movement components. In the Behavior Tree and StateTree versions twelve drones fly the whole hall, and in the Mass version a crowd of 200 follows a beacon through it. Open it from the demo menu. GPU voxelization checks itself. With Voxelization Method set to Auto , each machine tests its GPU before building navigation on it. There is a capability check, a self-test through the real pipeline (run once per GPU, driver and build, then remembered), and spot checks while the game runs. If the GPU fails, the plugin voxelizes on the CPU for the rest of the session. The log says which check failed and why, and the manager's On Voxelization Changed event fires. Voxelization Method set to GPU stays on the GPU. See the Settings reference . Improved Better fish swimming. Fish hold their depth and climb by pointing their nose up instead of sliding up and down. They stay upright, school side by side and in layers, and turn away from walls straight away. The tail beats with the swimming speed ( Tail Beat From Speed in the Flight Config), and a skeletal fish's swim animation plays at the same rate. See Flight and locomotion . Drones and hunters. Drones no longer bob up and down over a perch or a landing pad. Engage holds a firing position until its target leaves it, flies to it in formation and leads a crossing target. Hunters remember what they lose sight of and search for it, and gliding birds land from where they are. See Behaviour nodes . Fixes GPU navigation on more graphics cards. On some GPUs and drivers (first reported on a laptop RTX 3060) the GPU-built navigation could come back incomplete and agents stood still. The GPU build now checks its own output word by word, rewrites anything that did not get written and rebuilds what it cannot repair. This applies to D3D12, D3D11 and Vulkan. Water and triggers no longer count as walls. The agents' own checks treated a Water Volume or an overlap-only trigger as solid. In water this meant fish found no cover, an ROV found no viewpoint and turtles found no seabed. Agent, tactical, EQS and path-smoothing checks now count only collision that blocks, and cover, firing and vantage points are chosen inside the navigation volume. Obstacles that jump back to the start of their track. When a moving obstacle reset to the start of its path (a loop that jumps back), the plugin read it as moving very fast. Its update was dropped and the space it had left stayed blocked. The plugin now handles the jump correctly. No crash without a renderer. A dedicated server, or any run with -nullrhi , crashed on a streamed level because navigation data was sent to a GPU that wasn't there. Thirty fixes from a code audit. A review of the whole plugin fixed thirty defects across Fly To, crowds, flight, streaming and replication, and the plugin now logs under its own category ( LcmNavigationLog ). LCM Nav3D 3.5.0 This release added landing, hunting, hiding and investigating, and made the plugin much smaller. It has behaviour nodes for flying agents (Engage, Investigate, Flee, Scan Area, Perch, Land and Take Off) for Behavior Trees, StateTree and Mass crowds, six new demo levels, eight Feature Examples levels, fish that behave in your own aquarium, and the demo levels became a free download from inside the editor. New A QuickStart level inside LCM Nav3D. /LCMNav3D/QuickStart/QuickStart opens with nothing else installed: a flying agent planning over and under obstacles, agent size, a patrol, and paths queried from Blueprint. Each display shows what it is checking while it runs. Walk up to a display to start it; O shows the planned routes. See Installation . Behaviour nodes: Engage, Investigate, Flee, Scan Area, Perch. Ready-made behaviours for flying agents, each as a Behavior Tree task, a StateTree task and a Mass crowd task. Engage Target finds a firing position and keeps line of sight; Investigate searches around a last-known position; Flee breaks line of sight and hides; Scan Area sweeps a volume; Perch lands on tagged ledges and pads. Agents in a crowd share the work: no two take the same perch, cover or vantage point. See Behaviour nodes . Land and Take Off. Drones descend vertically, birds and fish glide in with a braking flare, and both can land on moving surfaces such as a rolling ship's deck or a moving lorry, or under a roof. New EQS generators and tests find landing sites for flying agents, and Engage can take its sightings from AI Perception. Six new demo levels, and a new demo menu. Hunter Drone, Harbour, Sea Cliffs, Coral Reef, Warehouse and Sentry Drones, each in Behavior Tree, StateTree and Mass editions, from a new menu with previews. They run without Lumen, so they perform well in any project. Feature Examples: eight levels

d: Why Unreal's Recast navmesh cannot represent open air, where each flying-AI workaround breaks down, and when volumetric SVO navigation is the right answer instead.
b: Documentation / Getting Started / Nav3D vs Recast LCM Nav3D vs Recast: navigation for flying AI Applies to LCM Nav3D 3.6.0 · Unreal Engine 5.2 to 5.8 · Updated 22 November 2026 In short: Unreal's Recast navmesh tells an agent "where can I stand?" . LCM Nav3D tells it "where is there empty air?" . They do different jobs. If your project has both soldiers and aircraft, you will usually run both, and Tutorial 09 shows how. Read this page if you are not sure which one you need. If you already know you need 3D navigation, go straight to Installation . How they differ Recast builds a surface . It is a mesh of convex polygons laid over the ground, and every point on it is a place where an agent could stand. LCM Nav3D builds a volume . It is a sparse voxel octree that divides up the empty space in the level, so a valid position is anywhere an agent fits, even 200 metres up with nothing below it. You cannot get the second from the first by changing settings. A navmesh only stores surfaces, so it has no way to say that a block of sky is free to fly through. Core Concepts explains how the octree stores that space, and why open sky takes up so little memory. Recast navmesh (ships with UE5) LCM Nav3D Represents the walkable surface the navigable volume Data structure convex polygon mesh, in tiles sparse voxel octree Answers where can I stand? where is there empty air? Movement across the ground any direction, including straight up Memory driven by the surface area you cover the amount of geometry in the level Natural fit soldiers, vehicles, characters drones, dragons, submarines, spacecraft Cost free, built in a plugin Common workarounds and their limits Most teams try one of these before they look at 3D navigation. Some of them are the right choice for some projects, so each one is described below with where it stops working. A navmesh plane at flight altitude You put an invisible floor at 3000 units and let Recast build on it. This is cheap and it works as long as every agent flies at that one height. As soon as an agent has to dive under a bridge or climb over a building, it can't. Paths are still 2D, and there is no way to avoid things above or below. Several stacked navmeshes This adds more layers, and more work. You have to author the transitions between layers by hand. An agent also can't fly diagonally through the space between two layers, and for a flying agent that is most of the space. A uniform 3D grid A voxel grid does store volume, and A* on it works. The problem is memory. It grows with the cube of the level size, and empty sky costs as much as solid rock, so a 2 km level needs far too much. An octree fixes this: one large node can cover a big empty area, and it only subdivides near geometry. Raycast steering with no pathfinding You fire a few traces and steer away from whatever they hit. It is cheap and looks fine in open terrain. It breaks on concave shapes like a U-shaped canyon, a hangar with one door or a courtyard. Steering has no plan for the whole route, so the agent flies into the pocket and gets stuck there. Problems like this often only show up late in a project. Hand-authored spline highways Splines are predictable, cheap and easy to art-direct. For scripted flypasts and fixed patrol routes they are the right tool, and you don't need pathfinding for those. Agents on splines can't go to a goal you didn't plan for, though, and every new route has to be made by hand. When Recast is the right answer Recast is mature, free, well tested and already works with Behavior Trees, EQS and the crowd system. Use it when: Your agents walk. That covers most games, and LCM Nav3D adds nothing for walking characters. Your agents only look like they fly , for example a drone that hovers 50 cm above the floor and follows the terrain. Recast with a Z offset is simpler and cheaper. Flight routes are fixed and scripted. Use splines. You need Detour crowd avoidance for a ground army. That is Recast's UCrowdManager , and it works well. When you need 3D navigation Agents fly through open space and have to find their way through gaps, such as canyons, caves, asteroid fields or the air between city buildings. Multi-level interiors where above and below both matter, and an agent should be able to choose between them. Underwater or zero-gravity movement, where there is no floor to project onto. You need tactical queries (cover, line of sight, height advantage) about points in the air as well as on the floor. Agents must reroute around things that move, in three dimensions. What you get besides pathfinding You can write 3D A* over a grid in a weekend. Flying agents need a lot more than that before they behave well in a game, and the plugin includes it: Capability What it does Chapter Volumetric EQS Generators and tests that score candidate points anywhere in the navigable volume, using SVO line-of-sight, cover, threat exposure and height advantage Tactical EQS Mass Entity crowds Thousands of agents through the ECS with no per-agent controller, tick function or code Mass Entity Crowds Dynamic obstacles Moving actors restamp the octree, and agents reroute around closing doors and rising platforms Dynamic Obstacles 3D nav links and area modifiers Vertical ladders, jump shafts and teleporters, plus volumetric cost overlays for water and danger zones Nav Links and Areas 6-DOF flight dynamics A rigid-body flight and swim model (thrust, lift, drag and attitude), so agents move like real bodies with weight Flight and Locomotion Gameplay Debugger integration Per-agent and plugin-wide state in the stock UE debugger, next to Recast, BT and EQS Gameplay Debugger Editor tooling A setup wizard, a health check that reports what would stop agents moving, and an auto-tuner that measures voxel settings against your real routes Editor Tools Running both in one level Most projects with flying agents also have walking ones, and the plugin is built for that. b: Documentation / Getting Started / Installation Tutorial 01: Installation Applies to LCM Nav3D 3.6.0 · Unreal Engine 5.2 to 5.8 · Updated 22 November 2026 In short: Put the plugin in YourProject/Plugins/LCMNav3D/ , open the project and let it compile, enable Show Plugin Content in the Content Browser, then open the QuickStart level and press Play. If its displays pass, your install is good. The demo levels are a free download from the LCM Nav3D menu. Time: ~10 minutes (plus one compile). Before you start Requirement Detail Unreal Engine 5.2 to 5.8 Platform Windows 64-bit or Linux Project type C++ project for a manual install (see below) Compiler Visual Studio 2022 with the Game development with C++ workload (Windows) The plugin comes as source code, so it has to be compiled once. How that happens depends on how you install it. Method A: Installed from Fab / Epic Games Launcher This is the easiest way, and it works with Blueprint-only projects . Install the plugin from the Launcher's Library → Fab Library section. It lands in <Engine>/Plugins/Marketplace/LCMNav3D/ and is already compiled for that engine version. Open your project. Edit → Plugins , search "LCM Nav3D", tick Enabled if it isn't already. Restart the editor when prompted. Skip to Verify the install . Method B: Manual install into your project Use this when you have the plugin as a folder (for example from a direct purchase or a version you re-targeted yourself). Close the editor. Copy the LCMNav3D folder into your project so the layout is: YourProject/ YourProject.uproject Plugins/ LCMNav3D/ LCMNav3D.uplugin Source/ Content/ Config/ Shaders/ Create the Plugins folder if your project doesn't have one. The folder must be named exactly LCMNav3D , because the content mount /LCMNav3D/ depends on it. If your project is Blueprint-only, convert it to C++ first. A Blueprint-only project has no build pipeline and cannot compile a source plugin. The easiest conversion: Tools → New C++ Class → None → Create Class . The editor generates a Source/ folder and restarts. You never have to write any C++ afterwards. Right-click YourProject.uproject → Generate Visual Studio project files . Open the generated .sln and build Development Editor | Win64 , or open the .uproject and click Yes when the editor offers to rebuild. The plugin is EnabledByDefault , so it turns itself on. Confirm under Edit → Plugins . Verify the install Do these in order. Each one catches a different kind of failure. 1. The plugin loaded Edit → Plugins → AI Navigation category. You should see LCM Nav3D , enabled, version 3.6.0. 2. Get the demo levels (optional) The demo levels, their art and the demo menu are a free download, LCM Nav3D Samples (about 0.9 GB to download, 1.3 GB installed). Your game does not need them. To install them: LCM Nav3D toolbar menu → Get the Demo Levels (free)... (or Demo Levels (free) on the Welcome screen) → Download and Install . The window shows the progress; you can pause, resume or cancel, and an interrupted download resumes where it stopped. Every file is checked before it is installed, into YourProject/Plugins/LCMNav3DSamples . When it finishes, Open the Demo Menu . Updates and removal: the same window offers a newer version when one is published, and Remove Samples . Both finish when the editor next starts. Nothing in LCM Nav3D refers to the samples. 3. You can see the demo content Plugin content is hidden by default in the Content Browser: Content Browser → Settings (the gear icon) → tick "Show Plugin Content". An LCM Nav3D Content folder appears in the tree (and LCM Nav3D Samples Content once the demo levels are installed). Without this you won't find the QuickStart level or any demo map. If it looks like the plugin didn't install, check this setting first. 4. A level runs Open LCM Nav3D Content → QuickStart → QuickStart (or QuickStart Level on the Welcome screen) and press Play . Walk up to a display to start it. One agent flies over and under obstacles, a large and a small agent take different routes, a patrol loops, and a Blueprint queries paths. Each display shows PASSED when its check succeeds. Press O to see the planned routes. With the demo levels installed, open LCM Nav3D Samples Content → Demo → MainMenu , press Play and pick a level. Demo → MainMenu is a gallery of every demo in the plugin, if you would rather browse than open maps by name. If that works, your install is correct and you can move on to Tutorial 02: Core Concepts . The engine plugins it turns on LCMNav3D.uplugin lists these as dependencies, so the engine turns them on for you. You don't need to change anything, but you should know they are enabled: Plugin Why it's needed StateTree , GameplayStateTree The StateTree task/condition/evaluator set MassEntity , MassGameplay , MassAI The Mass crowd layer SmartObjects Smart Object behaviour definitions DataValidation In-editor validation of illegal Mass trait combinations If the plugin fails to load with GetLastError 126 , one of the Mass plugins got disabled. MassGameplay in particular is required at runtime. Re-enable it and restart. d: How LCM Nav3D carves empty air into a sparse voxel octree and paths through it. Covers the navigation manager actor, world extent, voxel size and clearance.
b: Documentation / Getting Started / Core Concepts Tutorial 02: Core Concepts Applies to LCM Nav3D 3.6.0 · Unreal Engine 5.2 to 5.8 · Updated 22 November 2026 In short: LCM Nav3D splits the empty space in your level into a tree of boxes (a Sparse Voxel Octree) and finds paths through the empty ones. You place one LcmNavigationManagerSVO actor per level, tell it how big your world is and how small the tightest gap is, and it handles the rest. Time: about 10 minutes of reading. You don't change anything in your project. The settings in later chapters will be easier to follow after this one. 1. Why not just use Unreal's navmesh? Unreal's Recast navmesh is a surface . It answers "where can I stand?" by covering the walkable parts of your level with polygons. That works well for a soldier. It doesn't work for a dragon, because a flying agent needs to know about the space above the ground, and the navmesh has nothing there. LCM Nav3D answers a different question: "where is there empty space?" It stores the volume of the level instead of the floor. Most of the rest of the plugin is about making that quick to build and quick to search. 2. The Sparse Voxel Octree, in one picture Imagine a giant cube around your level. Now: Is the cube completely empty? Yes → done, one big box of free space. No , something's in it? → cut it into 8 smaller cubes and ask each one the same question. Repeat until the cubes reach your minimum size. The result of those steps is the octree. Big empty region Region with a wall in it ┌───────────────────┐ ┌─────────┬─────────┐ │ │ │ empty │ empty │ │ │ ├────┬────┼─────────┤ │ ONE node. │ │ ▓▓ │ e │ empty │ ▓▓ = solid, keeps │ Done. │ ├────┼────┤ │ subdividing │ │ │ e │ ▓▓ │ │ e = empty, stops └───────────────────┘ └────┴────┴─────────┘ Sparse means open sky takes very little memory, because one node can cover a huge volume. The octree only gets detailed near geometry. So a 2 km map doesn't need memory for every cubic metre. Most of it is empty air, which is stored in a few large nodes. What this means for you: the size of your navigation data depends mostly on how much geometry your level has , and much less on how big the level is. 3. The one actor you must place LcmNavigationManagerSVO : place one in your level. You need exactly one per level. It holds the octree, runs the pathfinder and answers every query. Every agent uses it, so if it isn't in the level, nothing can navigate. Its Details panel is sorted in the order you should set things up: Category What it's for 1. Setup Finite or infinite world, the biggest decision 2. Voxels Size and resolution 3. Collision Which geometry counts as an obstacle 4. Performance Frame-budget knobs 5. Debug Visualisation 6. Runtime State Read-only live info Every field is described in the Settings Reference . This page only covers the ideas behind them. 4. Finite vs Infinite This is 1. Setup → Infinite World . It is the most important choice, and it changes which other settings are shown. Finite (default, Infinite World unticked) One fixed box of navigation, built once. You set WorldExtent (default 10000 cm = a 200 m cube, since extent is measured from the centre outward). Built at BeginPlay if Auto Build On Play is on (it is by default). Simple, fast and predictable. Use this for: arenas, levels, dungeons, single buildings, anything with a boundary. Start here. Most projects never need anything else. Infinite ( Infinite World ticked) The world is divided into chunks of ChunkSize (default 8000 cm ). Chunks are generated around your agents as they move and thrown away behind them. Use this for: open worlds, streaming levels, procedural terrain, anything without a boundary. It is more complicated, because a chunk has to be generated before an agent can route through it. Be careful with ChunkSize . It affects memory, and it also affects whether long routes can be found at all. 8000 is the tested default. Only change it if you have a reason, and test again afterwards. Larger chunks mean fewer but heavier builds. Smaller chunks mean more, lighter builds and more seams for routes to cross. 5. Resolution settings MinVoxelSize (default 100 cm ) How small the smallest box can get. This setting has the biggest effect on both path quality and cost. Smaller → finds tighter gaps, uses more memory, takes longer to build. Larger → cheaper and faster, but narrow openings vanish and agents route around them. Note: this is a lower limit. The octree keeps halving its boxes, so the real leaf size is the world (or chunk) size divided by two again and again until it gets close to MinVoxelSize . That has two effects you might not expect: Changing MinVoxelSize from 100 to 90 may change nothing (same number of halvings). Changing it from 100 to 60 may cross a threshold and double your memory in one step. Test your changes. The leaf size you get is usually not the exact number you typed in. Rule of thumb: set MinVoxelSize to roughly half the narrowest gap your agents must fly through. A 3 m window needs about 150 cm or finer. ClearancePadding (default 100 cm ) Grows obstacles by this much when voxelizing, so agents don't clip walls. Note: if you set this too high, your level gets sealed off. When the padding gets close to the voxel size, doorways and corridors fill in completely, and the pathfinder reports "no route" through an opening you can clearly see. Keep ClearancePadding well below MinVoxelSize . If you need more clearance than that, lower MinVoxelSize too. If agents refuse to path through an opening, this setting is the first thing to check. 6. How a path is found For a short hop, it's a straight search through the octree. For anything longer, there are two levels: 1. MACRO: "which chunks/regions do I cross?" (coarse, cheap, long-range) ↓ 2. MICRO: "which voxels inside them?" (fine, detailed, short-range) ↓ 3. SMOOTH: turn the blocky voxel path into a nice line This happens automatically, so you don't call these steps yourself. It is still useful to know a

d: Build a pawn that flies through true 3D space to a goal in Unreal Engine, using a navigation manager, an AIController and one LCM Fly To task. No C++ needed.
b: Documentation / Getting Started / Your First Flying Agent Tutorial 03: Your First Flying Agent Applies to LCM Nav3D 3.6.0 · Unreal Engine 5.2 to 5.8 · Updated 22 November 2026 In short: You need three things: an LcmNavigationManagerSVO in the level, a pawn with an AIController , and a Behavior Tree whose only task is LCM Fly To (SVO) pointed at a blackboard key. No C++. Time: ~20 minutes. You'll end with: a pawn that flies through 3D space to a goal in your own level. What we're building Level ├── LcmNavigationManagerSVO ← navigation (one per level) ├── BP_MyFlyer (Pawn) ← the flying pawn │ └── AIController: BP_MyFlyerAI │ └── runs BT_MyFlyer │ └── Blackboard: BB_MyFlyer (Vector key "GoalLocation") └── TargetPoint ← where we want it to go Step 1: Add the navigation manager In the Place Actors panel, search LcmNavigationManagerSVO . Drag one into your level. Position doesn't matter much. It uses its own location as the centre of the navigation volume, so put it roughly in the middle of your playable space. Select it and set, in the Details panel: Category Field Value 1. Setup Infinite World unticked (finite, see Tutorial 02 ) 1. Setup Auto Build On Play ticked 2. Voxels World Extent large enough to cover your play space (default 10000 = 200 m cube) 2. Voxels Min Voxel Size 100 to start 2. Voxels Clearance Padding 100 to start World Extent measures outward from the actor , so 10000 gives you a 200 m cube centred on the manager. If your agents will fly outside that box, increase it: outside the volume there is no navigation data and paths will fail. See what it built Tick 5. Debug → Draw Debug Volumes and press Play. You'll see the octree drawn over your level, with big boxes in open air and small ones packed around geometry. Use this a lot while you tune your settings. If a doorway you care about has no small voxels in it, the pathfinder can't use it either. Turn it off again when you're done, because it is slow to draw. Step 2: Make the pawn You need something that can move in 3D without gravity. Content Browser → Add → Blueprint Class → Pawn . Name it BP_MyFlyer . Open it and add a Floating Pawn Movement component. (Add Component → search "Floating Pawn Movement".) This is what makes it fly rather than fall. Select FloatingPawnMovement and set Max Speed to 600 . Match this to the task's Flight Speed later. Add a Static Mesh component so you can see it. A cone or sphere is fine. Scale it down to something sensible. In Class Defaults , set Auto Possess AI to Placed in World or Spawned . Collision tip. For your first test, set the mesh's collision to No Collision . When physics and navigation work against each other, the agent often jitters or gets stuck, and you want your first test to be simple. Turn collision back on once flying works. Step 3: Blackboard and Behavior Tree The blackboard Add → Artificial Intelligence → Blackboard . Name it BB_MyFlyer . Add one key: Type: Vector , Name: GoalLocation The Fly To task also accepts an Object key holding an Actor. Use a Vector for now; the Actor form is what you'd use for chasing, covered at the end. The behavior tree Add → Artificial Intelligence → Behavior Tree . Name it BT_MyFlyer . Open it, and in the Details panel set Blackboard Asset to BB_MyFlyer . Drag from ROOT and add a Sequence . Drag from the Sequence and add the task named Fly To ; it appears in the tree as LCM Fly To (SVO) . Select that task and set: Field Value Blackboard Key GoalLocation Acceptance Radius 100 Flight Speed 600 Leave everything else at defaults for now. Figure 03.1: where LCM Fly To (SVO) goes. This is the BT_FlightBehavior demo that comes with the plugin. It is a little more than what you just built. It uses the same Fly To task, with a goal picker before it and a retry-with-delay branch next to it, so the tree keeps going when a plan fails. Your tree only needs the highlighted node to start flying. The FlyTo settings, in full You won't need most of these at first. It still helps to know how the panel is laid out before you look for a specific setting. Figure 03.2: the LCM Fly To task and its six sections. 1 Goal is where the agent goes. 2 Movement controls how it flies there. 3 Pathfinding controls how the route is planned. 4 Avoidance handles other agents and walls. 5 Moving Goal is only for chasing something that moves, and 6 Streaming is only used in an infinite world. Two fields change which other fields you see: Use Flight Movement Component : when it is ticked, section 2 is hidden, because the movement component handles speed and dynamics instead of the task. Avoidance Style : when it is set to CBS , the seven tuning fields under it are hidden. CBS works inside the planner and doesn't use them. The panel hides any setting that the current setup ignores. So every setting you can see is one that is being used. Step 4: The AI Controller Add → Blueprint Class → AIController . Name it BP_MyFlyerAI . Open it. On the Event BeginPlay node: Add Run Behavior Tree , set BTAsset to BT_MyFlyer . We need to put a goal in the blackboard. Still on BeginPlay, after Run Behavior Tree: Add Get Blackboard → Set Value as Vector . Key Name: GoalLocation Value: for a first test, drag in a Get Actor Of Class node with Actor Class = TargetPoint , then GetActorLocation from it. BeginPlay ─→ Run Behavior Tree (BT_MyFlyer) └→ Set Value as Vector (Key: GoalLocation, Value: GetActorOfClass(TargetPoint).GetActorLocation) Compile and save. Go back to BP_MyFlyer → Class Defaults → set AI Controller Class to BP_MyFlyerAI . Step 5: Fly Drag a TargetPoint into your level, somewhere your flyer has to climb or go around geometry to reach. Put it up high so you can see the agent fly in 3D. Drag BP_MyFlyer into the level, somewhere with open air around it. Press Play . Your pawn should take off and fly to the target point, routing around geometry in full 3D. If it doesn't move Go through this list from the top. The causes are in the order you are likely to run into them. Symptom Cause Fix Output

d: Author identical 3D flight behaviour in StateTree instead of a Behavior Tree. Swap RunBehaviorTree for a StateTreeAIComponent and bind the Fly To task target.
b: Documentation / Getting Started / The Same Agent in StateTree Tutorial 04: The Same Agent in StateTree Applies to LCM Nav3D 3.6.0 · Unreal Engine 5.2 to 5.8 · Updated 22 November 2026 In short: This builds the same flying agent as Tutorial 03 , but in StateTree instead of a Behavior Tree. Swap the AIController's RunBehaviorTree for a StateTreeAIComponent , and bind the Fly To task's TargetLocation instead of a blackboard key. Time: ~15 minutes. Do Tutorial 03 first . This chapter only covers the differences. Should you use StateTree or Behavior Tree? Both are fully supported and give the same flight. They can do the same things, so use the one you prefer working in. Behavior Tree StateTree Goal comes from A blackboard key Bound instance data on the task Best at Reactive priority ordering Explicit states and transitions Maturity Stable Epic's StateTree plugin is experimental on 5.2, stable from 5.3 The 5.2 caveat. Epic's StateTree plugin is experimental on 5.2. If you're shipping on 5.2 and want the most conservative option, use the Behavior Tree path. On 5.3+ this distinction disappears. Step 1: The pawn Exactly as Tutorial 03 Step 2 : a Pawn with Floating Pawn Movement , a visible mesh, and Auto Possess AI = Placed in World or Spawned . Nothing StateTree-specific here. Step 2: Create the StateTree asset Content Browser → Add → Artificial Intelligence → StateTree . When it asks for a schema , choose StateTree AI Component Schema . You need this schema, because it gives the Fly To task the AI context (controller and pawn) it uses. Name it ST_MyFlyer . Step 3: Add the Fly To task Open ST_MyFlyer . You'll have a Root state. Add a child state and name it FlyToGoal . With that state selected, in the Tasks section click + and choose Fly To (listed under the LCM Nav3D category). Set the task's properties: Field Value Notes Target Location your goal See binding below Acceptance Radius 100 Flight Speed 600 Match your Floating Pawn Movement Max Speed Binding the goal This is the main difference from Behavior Trees. There is no blackboard, so you bind the task's Target Location to a value instead. The simplest approach is a StateTree parameter : Select the Root state → in Parameters , add a parameter: Name GoalLocation , Type Vector . Select the Fly To task → click the bind icon next to Target Location → choose GoalLocation . Now anything that sets that parameter drives the agent. Chasing instead. The task also has a Target Actor field. Set or bind that and the agent chases the actor, using the same prediction logic as the BT version. Note the ST chase path requires Target Actor to be non-null. If you want a fixed point, use Target Location . Why Fly To has its own Target Actor field This often confuses people who come from Behavior Trees. The field doesn't replace Find Actor By Tag . It is where you connect the output of Find Actor By Tag . A Behavior Tree has a blackboard, so a BT task can name a key and read whatever wrote it. StateTree has no blackboard. Data moves by property binding from one node's output to another node's input, which means the consuming node must declare a field to receive the value. Delete Target Actor and there is nothing left to bind to. Unreal does the same thing in its own tasks. Epic's Move To task has the same pair of fields: a Destination vector and an optional Target Actor . If both are set, the actor is used. Fly To needs the actor itself, not just a position, because it reads the target's location and velocity every tick to aim ahead of it. With a single position, the agent would fly to where the target was when the state started. Resolve the actor with the evaluator, not the task Two nodes can find an actor by tag. One finds it once, and the other keeps it up to date: Find Actor By Tag (task) Find Actor By Tag (evaluator) Resolves Once, on state entry Continuously, on Refresh Interval Found Actor Location Frozen at entry Refreshed every tick Target destroyed / respawns Stays stale until re-entry Re-resolves immediately Costs a state Yes - unless Stay Running After Resolve lets it share one No Visible to Nodes ordered after it The whole subtree of the state it sits on Can fail a state Yes (returns Failed ) No - gate on its b Found Actor output Prefer the evaluator for goal sources. Put it on the parent state, set Tag to Player , and bind Fly To 's Target Actor to its Found Actor . One resolver then feeds Fly To , Look At , conditions and transitions at once, and it stays correct when the target dies or streams in late. Only the search is throttled by Refresh Interval (0.5 s by default); the location output refreshes every tick from the cached pointer, so a moving target is always current. Use the task form when you want the value fixed on entry, for example to pick a patrol anchor and stick with it. Also use it when you want the state to fail if no actor has the tag. Roaming between tagged goals. The task form also has Pick Random Match : tag every goal actor in the level (say, Goal ), put the task ahead of Fly To in one state, and tick Stay Running After Resolve . That option lets the two tasks share a state. If it is off, the find task finishes on entry , and when one task finishes, its whole state finishes. Fly To is entered but never ticked, and the agent doesn't move. Bind Fly To's Target Location to Found Actor Location . Then add an On State Completed transition back into the same state. Make it a Go to State transition that targets the state itself, not Tree Succeeded , which would end the whole run after the first leg. Each time the state is entered again it picks a new random goal. Avoid Repeat Pick (on by default) makes sure it is never the goal the agent is already at. Every agent runs its own copy of the tree, so a crowd using one StateTree asset spreads out over the goals by itself. The Pick Random Goal task works the same way with random points instead of placed actors, and it has the same Stay Running After Resolve option for the same reason. Figu

d: Add a Dynamic Obstacle component to any moving actor. LCM Nav3D restamps the octree and agents reroute live around doors, platforms and destructible cover.
b: Documentation / Getting Started / Dynamic Obstacles Tutorial 05: Dynamic Obstacles Applies to LCM Nav3D 3.6.0 · Unreal Engine 5.2 to 5.8 · Updated 22 November 2026 In short: Add an LCM Nav3D Dynamic Obstacle component to any actor that moves. It updates the octree as the actor moves, and agents reroute around it. Use it for closing doors, rising platforms, patrolling hazards and destructible cover. Time: ~15 minutes. Assumes Tutorial 03 . Static vs dynamic When the navigation volume is built, all static geometry is baked into it. That keeps queries fast, but the bake doesn't change when things move. Never moves? Do nothing. It's already in the octree. Moves? It needs a Dynamic Obstacle component, or the octree will keep believing the space is empty and agents will fly straight through it. A common mistake is to move a static-mesh actor at runtime without the component. You get no error. Agents just ignore it, because the navigation data still has it where it started. Step 1: Make a moving obstacle Create a Blueprint Actor, BP_MovingWall . Add a Static Mesh component: a Cube, scaled so it really blocks a route (for example 400 × 100 × 400). Make sure the mesh has collision enabled . The voxelizer finds obstacles via collision, so a mesh set to No Collision is invisible to navigation. Step 2: Add the Dynamic Obstacle component In BP_MovingWall , Add Component → search "LCM Nav3D Dynamic Obstacle" . Nothing else is needed. The component registers itself with the navigation manager at BeginPlay and follows its owner from then on. The settings Field Default What it does Update Distance Threshold 50 cm How far the actor must move before the octree is updated. A larger value is cheaper, but the navigation falls further behind the actor. Tracked Components (empty) Empty means the whole actor . Pick specific components to track only part of it. Tracked Components is useful when only one part of an actor gets in the way, like a gate inside a decorative frame or a swinging arm on a fixed base. Pick just that component. Then only its movement updates the octree, and only its bounds block agents. You can also manage this at runtime from Blueprint with Add Tracked Component and Remove Tracked Component . Step 3: Move it Give it motion. The simplest version, in the Event Graph: Event Tick ─→ SetActorLocation( StartLocation + (0, sin(GameTime) * 700, 0) ) You can also use a Timeline, a Sequencer track or physics. The component watches the transform, so it works however the actor is moved. Step 4: See it work Place BP_MovingWall so it periodically seals the only route between your flyer and its goal. Press Play . The agent should path around the wall, and when the wall closes the route, re-plan and take a different way. To watch it happen: tick Draw Debug Volumes on the navigation manager. You'll see the voxels under the wall switch to blocked as it moves. How agents notice Agents re-plan automatically. The relevant setting is on the navigation manager : Field Default Meaning 4. Performance → Finite Obstacle Update Interval 0.1 s How often obstacle changes are folded into the finite-world octree Lower = more reactive, more CPU. 0.1 is a good balance. For fast-moving hazards where agents must react instantly, try 0.05 . Fly To sees obstacles coming The octree only says where an obstacle is . A Fly To agent (Behavior Tree or StateTree) also predicts where every Dynamic Obstacle will be and times its pass: a gate, piston or door on a cycle: it learns the cycle from the motion and replays it, so it knows when the gap opens; a spinning blade or sweeper: it turns the obstacle's own box about its pivot; anything else: its current velocity, trusted for a second or two; an obstacle that jumps back to the start of its track is treated as a jump, not as a sudden burst of speed. Using those predictions, the agent slows down, waits for a gap or takes a detour. If it can't get out of the way in time, it dodges. It picks the dodge by testing each possible escape with its own flight dynamics. Fly To field ( 4. Avoidance ) Default Meaning Avoid Moving Obstacles on Off = the agent learns of a mover only when the mover lands on its next waypoints Moving Obstacle Look-Ahead 3 s How far ahead the route is tested against the predictions Moving Obstacle Margin 50 cm Space kept between the agent's body and a mover r.LcmNav.MovingObstacles.Draw 1 draws the predictions in play. Which collision types count The octree is built from the collision types in the manager's Obstacle Query Channels (default WorldStatic + WorldDynamic ). A mover's collision object type must be in that list, or it never reaches the octree: Draw Debug Volumes shows the level but not the mover, and only the Fly To prediction keeps agents off it. Movers are usually WorldDynamic , so keep it in the list. Ready-made examples These demo maps show this working. Open any of them and read the setup: Map Shows Demo/BehaviourTree/PreBaked_FiniteMaps/DynObs_BT Obstacles sealing routes in a finite world Demo/BehaviourTree/InfniteMaps/DynObs_BT The same rig in a streaming infinite world Demo/BehaviourTree/InfniteMaps/DynObsTunnel_BT Movers sweeping a sealed tunnel: the wall-integrity test Demo/StateTree/InfniteMaps/DynObs_ST · DynObsTunnel_ST The StateTree equivalents Demo/MassEntity/PreBaked_FiniteMaps/DynObs_MassEntity Dynamic obstacles against a Mass crowd Demo/MassEntity/InfniteMaps/DynObs_Tunnel_MassEntity A crowd flowing through a tunnel as movers sweep it Demo/BehaviourTree/InfniteMaps/DynObs_Stress_BT · DynObs_Stress_ST · DynObs_Stress_MassEntity The Obstacle Gauntlet: 42 movers in six zones (gates, crossing traffic, windmills, pistons, head-on blocks, bouncers) The obstacles in these maps are driven along splines by the bundled BP_SplineMove Blueprint ( Content/Blueprints/ ), so you can look at a complete working setup instead of building one yourself. For a simpler ping-pong mover the plugin also ships the LCM Nav3D Obstacle Mover component, below. The Obstacle

d: Add one trait to a Mass Entity Config and a crowd navigates in full 3D through the Unreal ECS. No per-agent controller, no tick function and no code required.
b: Documentation / Going Further / Mass Entity Crowds Tutorial 06 - Mass Entity crowds (10K+ agents) Applies to LCM Nav3D 3.6.0 · Unreal Engine 5.2 to 5.8 · Updated 22 November 2026 Add one trait to a Mass Entity Config and a crowd can navigate in 3D. You don't need a controller for each agent, a tick function or any code. Time: ~20 minutes. You'll end with: thousands of agents flying to a goal. An actor-based AI agent with a controller, movement component and behaviour tree costs about 50 µs per tick, so a few hundred of them fill up the game thread. Mass stores agents as ECS fragments instead, and processes all of them in one pass. Prerequisites The MassEntity and MassGameplay plugins enabled. LCM Nav3D enables both; if you stripped them, re-enable both or the module fails to load. An LcmNavigationManagerSVO in the level with navigation built. If you have never used Mass, read Epic's "MassEntity Quick Start" first. This tutorial only adds a trait to the standard setup. Step 1: Create the agent config Add → Miscellaneous → Data Asset → MassEntityConfigAsset . Name it DA_MyCrowd . Open it and add three traits, one from each category: Trait Category Set LCM Nav3D Agent Movement - exactly one Nav Mode , Agent Radius , Max Speed LCM Nav3D Goal Goal Goal Mode , and the location or tag LCM Nav3D ISM Render Rendering Mesh Choosing a Nav Mode Nav Mode Use it for Cost Path Following Agents with different goals, precise routes, infinite worlds One path per agent Flow Field A crowd sharing one goal - the 10K-scale option One field, shared by everyone Note: add a rendering trait, or you won't see your agents. They spawn and navigate correctly but nothing is drawn, because the navigation trait only handles navigation. Most people run into this the first time. Useful movement settings Setting Default What it does Max Turn Rate Deg 360 Rounds off sharp corners into curves. 0 = turn instantly Max Acceleration 2000 cm/s². Together with turn rate, this gives the movement a sense of weight Flight Style Physics Physics (inertia) vs Linear (magic / biological, instant) Avoidance Style Reactive Reactive (boids) / Predictive (ORCA, smooth mutual passing) / None Lane Bias 0.6 Spreads a crowd across a corridor instead of balling up at turns The defaults already give natural-looking movement. Step 2: Spawn them Place a MassSpawner actor in the level. In Entity Types , reference DA_MyCrowd . Set Spawn Count . Start with 100 while you set it up. Give it a spawn-distribution asset so agents start at distinct positions inside your navigation volume . Step 3: Give them a goal The LCM Nav3D Goal trait does this with no code: Goal Mode Set Behaviour Fixed Location Goal Location Everyone paths to that point Tagged Actor Target Actor Tag (e.g. ApexGoal ) Everyone paths to the tagged actor, re-pathing if it moves Repath Tolerance Cm decides how far a moving target drifts before agents re-path; Arrival Tolerance Cm is where they stop. Setting a goal from code instead Write the goal and set the status. The processors handle everything after that. auto& Req = EntityManager.GetFragmentDataChecked<FLcmMassPathRequestFragment>(Handle); Req.Goal = TargetPos; Req.Status = ELcmMassPathStatus::Pending; Status moves Pending → InFlight → Complete (or Failed ) and is readable at any time, so your own logic can branch on it. Step 4: Check it works Press Validate Entity Config on the asset. It finds trait mistakes that give no error at runtime, where the only sign is that the agents don't move. Press Play with r.LcmNav.Mass.DebugDraw 1 . Agents are drawn as spheres coloured by status (grey idle, yellow pending, green complete, red failed) with a line to their waypoint. Scale up gradually: 100, then 1,000, then 10,000, watching frame time. If nothing moves Symptom Cause Fix Nothing visible at all No rendering trait Add LCM Nav3D ISM Render Spheres are red No path to the goal Goal is outside the navigation volume, or inside geometry Spheres stay grey No goal set Add the Goal trait, or write the request fragment Validation error on save Two movement traits, or Goal on a Flow Field agent See Mass Trait Reference Crowd vanishes when you walk away World Partition streamed the spawner out See the World Partition section of the trait reference Tuning These console variables switch features off or override them for the whole game. For normal setup, use the trait settings instead. CVar Default What it does r.LcmNav.Mass.MaxPathsPerTick 64 Spreads a large spawn wave's path requests across frames r.LcmNav.Mass.Avoidance 1 Master switch for inter-agent avoidance r.LcmNav.Mass.DebugDraw 0 Status-coloured spheres and waypoint lines Scope Mass agents resolve both endpoints within the agent's own chunk . Keep crowd goals in the same chunk as the crowd, or use a Behaviour Tree agent for long cross-chunk routes. Related Mass Trait Reference : every trait, which ones you can combine, and a World Partition problem to avoid. Tutorial 04 - StateTree , the per-entity AI layer that pairs with Mass.

d: LCM Nav3D ships EQS generators and tests that work in true 3D: candidate points anywhere in the navigable volume, scored by volumetric line-of-sight and cover.
b: Documentation / Going Further / Tactical EQS in True 3D Tutorial 07 - Authoring true-3D tactical EQS Applies to LCM Nav3D 3.6.0 · Unreal Engine 5.2 to 5.8 · Updated 22 November 2026 In short: LCM Nav3D ships EQS generators and tests that work in 3D . They generate candidate points anywhere in the navigable volume and score them by SVO line of sight, cover, threat exposure, LCM Nav3D path distance and height. You build a query from these nodes the same way as with stock EQS. The only differences are the Apex: -prefixed generators/tests and that "distance" means LCM Nav3D path , not Euclidean or navmesh. The LCM Nav3D EQS node catalog Generators ( UEnvQueryGenerator , produce 3D points): Node Produces LCM Nav3D | Points In SVO Volume uniform 3D points in an AABB, filtered to unblocked SVO leaves LCM Nav3D | Hemispherical Ring 3D shells around a target (perch / orbit / high-ground); Upper Hemisphere Only option LCM Nav3D | Points Along Path points sampled along the LCM Nav3D path between two contexts LCM Nav3D | Portal Proximity points at macro-graph portal centres near a context (chokepoints) Tests ( UEnvQueryTest , score/filter): Node Axis Notes LCM Nav3D | Line Of Sight 3D visible to context (bool) volumetric SVO LOS, not 2.5D LCM Nav3D | Reachability 3D an LCM Nav3D path exists (bool) filter unreachable candidates LCM Nav3D | Path Distance 3D LCM Nav3D path length (float) NOT Euclidean; Context = Querier LCM Nav3D | Threat Exposure summed SweepPenalty toward threats (float) lower = safer LCM Nav3D | Cover Score 3D fraction of threats occluded-from (float) higher = better cover LCM Nav3D | Height Advantage Z over context (float) high ground Contexts ( UEnvQueryContext ): Node Returns LCM Nav3D | Known Threats actors tagged ApexThreat LCM Nav3D | Threats From AI Perception the querier's perceived threats ( Tutorial 08 ) Step 1 - Author a sniper-perch query Create an EQS query EQS_FindSniperPerch : Generator: LCM Nav3D | Hemispherical Ring 3D - GenerateAround = the threat context (Known Threats / Threats From AI Perception), RadiusMin/Max = your engagement band, Upper Hemisphere Only = true (perch above the threat). Test: LCM Nav3D | Line Of Sight 3D (Context = threats) - Score, prefer should-have-LOS - a perch must see its target. Test: LCM Nav3D | Cover Score 3D (Context = threats) - Score↑ - partial cover is good. Test: LCM Nav3D | Height Advantage (Context = threats) - Score↑ - favour high ground. Test: LCM Nav3D | Reachability 3D (Context = Querier) - Filter - the agent must be able to get there. The best item is a high position the agent can reach, partly in cover, with line of sight to the threat, which makes it a good sniper perch. Figure 07.1: the parts of a Nav3D query. One generator makes candidate points, and then the tests score or filter them, from top to bottom. Here Apex: Points In SVO Volume makes unblocked 3D points over an 800×800×400 half-extent at 200 spacing. A floor-based generator can't do this, because it only knows about points on the ground. The two tests are colour-coded by role in the graph: a filter removes items, a score ranks them. The Details panel on the right belongs to the selected test: Test Purpose - Score Only , Filter Only , or both. This decides whether an item that fails the test is scored lower or removed . Context - what the test measures against . EnvQueryContext_LcmKnownThreats here, so line of sight is evaluated toward the threats the agent knows about. Agent Radius - how wide the thing that has to fit is. Set it to your real agent size. A perch that a 50 cm drone can reach may be too small for a 200 cm gunship. Scoring Equation and the Preview graph - the curve mapping raw measurement to score. The preview updates as you edit, so you can see how a Linear curve changes to Square before you run the query. Step 2 - The EQS Testing Pawn Drop an EQS Testing Pawn in the level, set its QueryTemplate to EQS_FindSniperPerch , and place threats so the contexts resolve. The candidate items render as colour-graded balls; tweak generator/test parameters and watch the scores update live. You only need UE's stock EQSTestingPawn . The LCM Nav3D nodes show up in it like any other EQS node. Step 3 - Wire the result into a Behavior Tree A Run EQS Query task/service runs EQS_FindSniperPerch and writes the best item to a blackboard Vector key. A MoveTo (or the LCM Nav3D FlyTo BT task) moves the agent to that key. Re-run on an interval (service) so the perch updates as threats move. (StateTree: run the query from a task that stores the location, then transition to your LCM Nav3D move task - see Tutorial 05.) Example queries Recipes you can build now from the catalog above: Query Recipe EQS_FindSniperPerch Hemispherical Ring 3D + Cover Score 3D + LOS 3D + Height Advantage EQS_FindFlankingApproach Points In SVO Volume + Threat Exposure↓ + Path Distance 3D EQS_FindAmbushCorner Portal Proximity + LOS 3D (prefer blocked) + Reachability 3D Related Tutorial 08 - perception-driven threat sources (the auto-populated threat context). Tutorial 05 - StateTree integration (the move side). ULcmTacticalQueryLibrary - the same primitives as Blueprint nodes ( Is Segment LOS Clear , Find Best Cover , Find Apex Path Sync , ...).

d: Wire Unreal's UAIPerceptionComponent into LCM Nav3D through the AI Perception Bridge, so perceived threats feed true-3D EQS queries for flanking and cover.
b: Documentation / Going Further / AI Perception Tutorial 08 - Perception-driven tactical AI Applies to LCM Nav3D 3.6.0 · Unreal Engine 5.2 to 5.8 · Updated 22 November 2026 In short: Add an LCM Nav3D AI Perception Bridge next to your agent's UAIPerceptionComponent → its perceived threats auto-feed the LCM Nav3D | Threats From AI Perception EQS context → a true-3D LCM Nav3D EQS query (volumetric candidate points + 3D-LOS / cover / threat-exposure tests) picks a flanking or cover position → your BT/StateTree moves the agent there. Mass crowds get the same via the LCM Nav3D Mass Perception Agent trait, which writes a perceived-threats fragment. Why you need it Tactical AI in Unreal usually goes through EQS, but the stock generators and tests are 2.5D (projected onto the navmesh). With them, a flying or multi-level NPC can't work out cover, line of sight or flanking in 3D. LCM Nav3D adds 3D EQS nodes, which place candidate points anywhere in the navigable volume and score them by SVO line of sight, cover and threat exposure. It also adds a bridge component , so the threats those tests use come straight from Unreal's own perception system. Prerequisites LCMNav3D plugin enabled, an ALcmNavigationManagerSVO with a built SVO in the level. An AI agent with an AAIController and a UAIPerceptionComponent configured with an AISense_Sight config (the standard UE setup - LCM Nav3D doesn't change this). Threats set up so perception can sense them (registered stimuli source / pawns on a hostile team), per your normal UE perception configuration. Part A - UActor agent (BT / StateTree) Step 1 - Add the perception bridge On your agent (the pawn or its controller - wherever the UAIPerceptionComponent lives), Add Component → "LCM Nav3D AI Perception Bridge" ( ULcmAIPerceptionBridge ). It auto-finds the owner's UAIPerceptionComponent on BeginPlay and subscribes to OnTargetPerceptionUpdated . DecayWindowSeconds (default 5 ): how long a threat stays in queries after the agent loses sight of it. Adjust it to suit your game. Nothing else needs connecting. Actors the agent senses are tracked, and lost ones are dropped after the decay time. That is all you need to connect perception to LCM Nav3D. Step 2 - Build the tactical EQS query Create an EQS query (e.g. EQS_FindFlankingApproach ) and assemble it from these nodes: Generator (pick one): Node Use it for LCM Nav3D | Points In SVO Volume general 3D candidate cloud around the agent LCM Nav3D | Hemispherical Ring 3D sniper-perch / high-ground / orbit candidates (set Upper Hemisphere Only ) LCM Nav3D | Points Along Path candidates strung along the LCM Nav3D path to a goal Tests (add several; set each one's Context to LCM Nav3D | Threats From AI Perception where it scores against threats): Node Purpose Typical setup LCM Nav3D | Threat Exposure prefer low summed danger toward threats Score, prefer less LCM Nav3D | Cover Score 3D prefer positions occluded from threats Score, prefer greater LCM Nav3D | Line Of Sight 3D filter to (or away from) visible-to-threat Filter LCM Nav3D | Reachability 3D drop positions the agent can't path to Filter (Context = Querier) LCM Nav3D | Path Distance 3D prefer near / far by LCM Nav3D path length Score (Context = Querier) LCM Nav3D | Height Advantage favour high ground over threats Score, prefer greater A good "flank to cover" query: Points In SVO Volume → Reachability 3D (filter) → Cover Score 3D (score↑) → Threat Exposure (score↓) → Path Distance 3D (score↓, mild weight). Every test that scores against threats gets them from the bridge through LCM Nav3D | Threats From AI Perception , so you don't need to tag anything by hand. (For non-perception workflows, LCM Nav3D | Known Threats returns actors tagged ApexThreat instead.) Step 3 - Wire it into BT or StateTree, then verify Behavior Tree: add a Run EQS Query service/task that runs your query and writes the result Vector / Actor to the blackboard, then a MoveTo (or an LCM Nav3D FlyTo ) to that key. StateTree: run the query from a task that stores the chosen location, then transition into your LCM Nav3D move task (see Tutorial 05). Verify in PIE: the agent should pick positions that it can reach, that are in cover from the threats it can see, and that are not very exposed to them. It should also stop reacting to a threat about 5 s after losing sight of it (the decay window). Walk a threat out of the sight cone and watch the chosen position shift once it decays. Part B - Mass crowd variant For crowd-scale tactical perception, use the native LCM Nav3D Mass perception (Tutorial 06 covers Mass setup): Add the LCM Nav3D Mass Perception Agent trait ( ULcmMassPerceptionTrait ) to your Mass entity config - set FactionId , SightRadius , FOVDegrees . Agents perceive different-faction agents within range + FOV + true-3D SVO line of sight . The ULcmMassPerceptionProcessor writes each agent's closest visible hostile into its FLcmMassPerceivedThreatsFragment ( ClosestThreatPos , bHasThreat , VisibleCount , LastSeenSeconds ). Read that fragment in your Mass logic (a StateTree task via UMassStateTreeProcessor , a steering processor, etc.) to drive evade / engage / regroup behaviour. Mass agents consume the perceived-threats fragment directly - they don't issue EQS queries (there is no Mass-native EQS querier). EQS tactical queries are the UActor path (Part A). If you want both, make your hero NPC an actor-based agent and query with Apex: Known Threats . Tag the threats the crowd cares about so the hero sees them too. What you build by hand All the nodes above are included and ready to use. Ready-made query assets are not included. You build your own from the generators and tests, and Tutorial 07 shows how. Four nodes need live flow-field or macro-graph state and are not available: the flow-field-directed generator, the flow-field-alignment test, the active-flow-field context, and the portal-proximity generator.
