d: Run walking agents on Recast and flying agents on the SVO in one level. The Crowd Avoidance Bridge lets Detour RVO steer Recast agents around LCM Nav3D pawns.
b: Documentation / Going Further / Hybrid Recast + Nav3D Tutorial 09 - Hybrid LCM Nav3D + Recast crowd avoidance Applies to LCM Nav3D 3.6.0 · Unreal Engine 5.2 to 5.8 · Updated 22 November 2026 In short: Add ULcmCrowdAvoidanceBridge to your LCM Nav3D flying pawn → stock UE5 UCrowdManager Detour RVO sees the LCM Nav3D pawn and steers Recast crowd agents around it. The Z-band filter (auto-applied by the bridge) prevents false-collision avoidance between agents at different vertical bands. Prerequisites The third-person template (or any project with a Character + AIController). LCMNav3D plugin enabled. An ALcmNavigationManagerSVO in the level. An ALcmFlyingPawn (or your own LCM Nav3D flying pawn). Step 1 - Add the bridge to your LCM Nav3D pawn In the editor, select your LCM Nav3D pawn → Add Component → search "LCM Crowd Avoidance Bridge". The defaults work for most pawns: bAutoRegister = true : registers with UCrowdManager on BeginPlay AgentRadius = 50 cm : a typical pawn radius AgentHalfHeight = 100 cm : the cylinder height Detour uses MaxSpeed = 800 cm/s : the same as the ULcmNavMovementComponent default Nothing else is needed on the LCM Nav3D side. Step 2 - Add Recast crowd agents (existing UE5 pattern) Your Recast ground crowd agents should already use UCrowdFollowingComponent instead of the default UPathFollowingComponent . This is the standard UE5 setup for any project using crowd avoidance, and LCM Nav3D doesn't change it. If you don't use UCrowdFollowingComponent yet: // In your AAIController subclass constructor GetCharacterMovement()->bUseAccelerationForPaths = true; // ...and override the AIController to use UCrowdFollowingComponent Or in Blueprint: the AIController's UCrowdFollowingComponent is auto-registered as the agent. Step 3 - Play Hit Play. Your LCM Nav3D flying pawn and Recast ground crowd agents now avoid each other (per the Z-band filter rules below). How the Z-band filter works Unreal's UCrowdManager Detour RVO assumes all agents are on one plane . Without a fix, a ground agent at Z=0 would treat a flying LCM Nav3D agent at Z=500 as a neighbour, and you would see the ground agent dodge something 5 metres above its head. The bridge fixes this with Detour's avoidance-group bits : Each agent gets an AvoidanceGroup bit derived from its world Z divided by r.LcmNav.Crowd.ZBandHeightCm (default 200 cm). Each agent's GroupsToAvoid is set to its own band + the ±1 adjacent bands (so vertically close agents still see each other). Cross-band agents (e.g. ground Z=0 and aerial Z=500 with 200 cm bands → bands 0 and 2) ignore each other via Detour's standard bitfield mask. This uses Detour's own group masks, so Detour itself doesn't need to be changed. Tuning r.LcmNav.Crowd.ZBandHeightCm Use case Recommended value Default (typical pawn-height scenes) 200 Low-ceiling interior (1.5m floors) 150 Vertical skyscraper (need fine-grained per-floor separation) 100 Open sky (most LCM Nav3D traffic is far above ground) 400 Disable filter (legacy Detour coplanar behaviour) 0 Change the CVar in PIE to try values, then put the one you like in your project's DefaultEngine.ini . Stacked multi-floor scenarios There is one UCrowdManager per world. When agents are on stacked floors (for example LCM Nav3D agents at Z=200, 500 and 800 sharing one UCrowdManager), the Z-band filter handles it. Any two agents more than one band apart ignore each other. If you want fully separate crowds, with each floor as its own crowd zone, you would need a separate UCrowdManager per zone, which means subclassing it in your project. The plugin doesn't do this for you. Performance notes Each registered LCM Nav3D bridge contributes ~1 RegisterAgent call at BeginPlay + ~7 virtual-call evaluations per Detour tick (Detour reads the ICrowdAgentInterface getters once per query). The Z-band filter removes most of the RVO work between bands (about 99 %). Only agents within one band of each other are included in each other's avoidance. Disabling the filter ( r.LcmNav.Crowd.ZBandHeightCm = 0 ) restores legacy Detour coplanar behaviour for benchmarking. Testing it by hand Spawn 5 Recast ground crowd agents in a circle at Z=0. Spawn 1 LCM Nav3D flying pawn with ULcmCrowdAvoidanceBridge at Z=500. Fly the LCM Nav3D pawn through the middle of the ground-agent circle. Expected : ground agents continue their pathing without dodging the airborne pawn (Z-band separation > 200cm default). Now fly the LCM Nav3D pawn down to Z=100 - ground agents dodge it. If step 4 fails (ground agents dodge the airborne pawn), check r.LcmNav.Crowd.ZBandHeightCm is not 0. What about the LCM Nav3D pawn's own avoidance? There are two ways to do it, and both work: LCM Nav3D CBS/ORCA (default, the FlyTo task's built-in steering): the LCM Nav3D pawn avoids Recast crowd agents via the existing CBS context. Detour Crowd is only used to tell the other agents where the LCM Nav3D pawn is. Use UCrowdFollowingComponent on the LCM Nav3D pawn : replace the LCM Nav3D pawn's AIController's UPathFollowingComponent with UCrowdFollowingComponent . The pawn then takes full part in Detour Crowd. It gets a suggested velocity from Detour and applies it through its movement component. Combine with ULcmNavMovementComponent for the locomotion side. Option 1 is the default. Option 2 is for projects that want the same crowd avoidance for LCM Nav3D and Recast agents. Mass variant A Mass Entity equivalent is not available in this release. Related LCM Nav3D classes LCM_BTTask_FlyTo - already has CBS+ORCA built-in for LCM Nav3D-internal avoidance LCM_BTTask_EvadeCBS - a defensive evade that uses the same CBS context ULcmNavMovementComponent - LCM Nav3D-aware flying-pawn movement component

d: Price 3D volumes per agent with stock NavArea classes and Navigation Query Filters: storms, preferred lanes, toll gates, no-fly zones, plus 3D NavLinks.
b: Documentation / Going Further / Cost Areas and NavLinks Tutorial 10 - Cost areas, query filters and 3D NavLinks Applies to LCM Nav3D 3.6.0 · Unreal Engine 5.2 to 5.8 · Updated 22 November 2026 In short: Drop an ALcmNavAreaModifier volume, give it a stock NavArea class, and every LCM Nav3D planner routes by it: FlyTo (BT and StateTree), Fly To Location, Mass crowds, FindPath and the stock Move To. A stock NavigationQueryFilter on the agent decides what each area costs that agent, or forbids it. ULcmNavLinkComponent places 3D ladders, drops and teleporters; link costs are queryable, and the planner does not route through links yet. What an area does A cost area is a volume (box, sphere or capsule) with a NavArea class. The planner reads three things from the class: NavArea field Effect on a route Default Cost Travel inside the area costs this many times the distance. 5.0 = five times dearer, 0.5 = a preferred lane. Fixed Area Entering Cost Paid once each time the route goes in. Use it for a toll or a doorway you want used sparingly. Default Cost at NavArea_Null 's level (1e30 or more) Impassable for everyone. No route crosses it. A query filter on an agent overrides those per class, the same way it does for Recast: a travel cost override, an entering cost override, or excluded . That way two agents can treat the same volume differently. For example, prey can avoid a predator's territory while the predator ignores it. Routes follow the cheapest total, not the shortest distance. An agent goes round a storm when going round is cheaper, and flies straight through when the detour costs more than the storm. Step 1 - Place a cost area Place an LCM Nav3D Nav Area Modifier (Volumetric) actor. Set Shape and scale the box to cover the volume. A sphere reads its radius from the extent's X. A capsule runs along local Z. Set Area Class . The plugin ships ready-made classes, and any stock or project NavArea subclass works: Class What it does LCM Nav Area - Storm (x5) Five times dearer inside. LCM Nav Area - Preferred Lane (x0.5) Half price: routes are drawn into it. LCM Nav Area - Toll Gate (+2000 to enter) Normal price inside, 2000 cm extra per entry. LCM Nav Area - Territory (priced by filters) Free for everyone, until a filter prices it. LCM Nav Area - Restricted (excluded by filters) Free, until a filter excludes it. LCM Nav Area - No-Fly (impassable) Nobody crosses it, under any filter. Leave Area Class empty to use Cost Multiplier on its own. That is the 3.3 behaviour, with no per-agent overrides. Overlaps. Where volumes overlap, an area the agent's filter excludes always wins. Otherwise the higher Priority decides the cost. Costs do not multiply. (They did before 3.4.) Moving areas. Attach the volume to anything that moves and tick Movable . Agents replan as it moves, and plan against where it will be over Prediction Seconds . Patrol moves a volume back and forth on its own, for demos and tests. After changing a class, shape, priority or size at runtime, call Notify Area Changed . Moving the actor needs no call. Step 2 - Give an agent a filter A filter is a stock NavigationQueryFilter Blueprint or class. Add Areas entries to override or exclude classes. The plugin ships two examples: LCM Nav Filter - Prey (Territory x10) and LCM Nav Filter - Civilian (Restricted excluded) . Agent Where the filter goes Pawn with an AI controller (BT, StateTree, Fly To Location) The controller's Default Navigation Filter Class . FlyTo reads it on every request. No task property is needed. A direct planner call FLcmNavigationQueryOptions::FilterClass . Mass crowd Navigation Filter on the LCM Nav3D Agent trait. Stock Move To Its Filter Class pin, as with Recast. With no filter, each area uses its own class defaults. Step 3 - See what an agent sees On the LCM Nav3D Manager , under 6. Debug > Cost Areas : Cost View : Regions draws each volume and what it costs. Heat tints the octree by price. Cost View Filter : which agent's filter the view uses. Set it to the prey's filter and the territory is highlighted. The console variable r.LcmNav.CostView 0|1|2 overrides the property while playing. The Gameplay Debugger's LCM category shows the selected agent's route cost: length, priced length, entering costs paid, and the areas it crosses. What happens at the edges Situation Result The goal is inside an area the agent's filter excludes The request fails: Get Last Path Cost Failure returns Goal In Excluded Area . Every way to the goal crosses an excluded area The request fails: No Route Under Filter . The agent starts inside an excluded area It is allowed out by the shortest way, then routes normally. An area moves across an agent's route FlyTo replans when the route's cost changes enough to matter. A FlyTo task reports these as Failed , with a Warning in the log, never an Error. Step 4 - Query costs yourself The query library prices a route the same way the planner does: // The travel multiplier at a point, and a route's cost, as a given filter sees them: bool bExcluded = false; const float Here = ULcmNavAreaQueryLibrary::GetCostMultiplierAtForFilter(this, Location, UMyPreyFilter::StaticClass(), bExcluded); float LengthCm, PricedCm, EnteringCost; bool bCrossesExcluded; ULcmNavAreaQueryLibrary::EvaluatePathCostForFilter(this, Waypoints, UMyPreyFilter::StaticClass(), LengthCm, PricedCm, EnteringCost, bCrossesExcluded); The filter-less versions ( GetCostMultiplierAt , GetCostMultiplierAlongPath ) read each area's own defaults. All of them are Blueprint-callable. 3D NavLinks UE's stock UNavLinkCustomComponent projects its ends onto a Recast navmesh. A flying pawn can use any two points in space, so LCM Nav3D ships ULcmNavLinkComponent for vertical ladders, drops and teleporters. Add the LCM Nav Link (3D Vertical) component to an actor. Set LinkStart and LinkEnd in world space, e.g. (0, 0, 0) and (0, 0, 800) . bBidirectional : climb up and slide down, or one way only. TraversalCostCm : the extra cost of using the link, e.g. 400 to f

d: LCM Nav3D adds its own category to Unreal's stock Gameplay Debugger. Press the debugger key in PIE, pick an agent and read per-agent and plugin-wide state live.
b: Documentation / Going Further / The Gameplay Debugger Tutorial 11 - LCMNav3D in the Gameplay Debugger Applies to LCM Nav3D 3.6.0 · Unreal Engine 5.2 to 5.8 · Updated 22 November 2026 In short: LCMNav3D ships an LCMNav3D category in the stock UE5 Gameplay Debugger. In PIE, press the standard Gameplay Debugger key (usually apostrophe ' ), select an agent, and the category shows that agent's state and the plugin's state next to Recast, BT, EQS and Perception. You don't have to set anything up in your project. It works as soon as the plugin is loaded. What it shows Plugin-wide block (always) == LCMNav3D == Manager: resolved Loaded chunks: 7 NavLink registry: 3 NavArea registry: 1 NavSystem bridge: active Field Meaning Manager Green when ALcmNavigationManagerSVO is in the world; red if missing Loaded chunks ActiveVirtualChunks.Num for infinite worlds; 1 for finite NavLink registry Count of ULcmNavLinkComponent currently registered NavArea registry Count of ALcmNavAreaModifier currently registered NavSystem bridge Green when the navigation-system proxy is registered with UNavigationSystemV1 Per-agent block (when an actor is selected) == Agent: BP_FlyingPawn_C_0 == Pos: X=1234.5 Y=678.9 Z=500.0 Speed: 624 cm/s Chunk: (0,0,0) full SweepPenalty: 0 Perceived: 2 (closest: BP_Enemy_C_1) Field Meaning Pos Pawn world location Speed Pawn->GetVelocity.Size in cm/s Chunk (IntVec3) resolution - full , coarse (low-resolution stub), or none (streaming gap) SweepPenalty Risk-field byte at the agent's location (0 to 255) Perceived Count of currently-perceived actors + closest threat name How to toggle In PIE, press the standard Gameplay Debugger key (usually apostrophe ' - check Project Settings → Engine → Gameplay Debugger if you've rebound it). The Gameplay Debugger HUD appears at the top of the viewport. Look for the LCMNav3D category - it should be enabled by default (state set to EnabledInGameAndSimulate at module init). Click an actor in the level to select it as the debug target - per-agent block populates. If the category isn't showing: Confirm you're in PIE (Gameplay Debugger only runs in PIE/Standalone, not the editor itself). Confirm the plugin is loaded (check Output Log for [LcmNavBridge] messages on map load). Confirm you're not in a Shipping/Test build (the category compiles out when WITH_GAMEPLAY_DEBUGGER=0 ). What survives PIE → editor → PIE reloads CVars (debug toggles, chase tuning, telemetry output and so on) stay set between PIE sessions and reset when you restart the editor. Profile loader state ( ULcmNavProfileSubsystem ) - re-applied on each PIE init if the profile path is in your project's startup. Telemetry buffer - flushed at module shutdown; survives PIE-stop but not editor-close. NavLink + NavArea registry - populated at each actor's BeginPlay ; PIE-stop clears via EndPlay . NavSystem bridge proxy - spawned per-world; new PIE session = new proxy. The Gameplay Debugger category itself stays on once the module has loaded . It keeps its registration between PIE sessions, because it is stored in the GameplayDebugger module's category list and not in the world. Adding your own fields To extend the category in your project subclass: #if WITH_GAMEPLAY_DEBUGGER class FProjectGameplayDebuggerCategory_Apex: public FGameplayDebuggerCategory_LcmNav3D { public: virtual void CollectData(APlayerController* PC, AActor* DebugActor) override { Super::CollectData(PC, DebugActor); // Gather project-specific state here } virtual void DrawData(APlayerController* PC, FGameplayDebuggerCanvasContext& Canvas) override { Super::DrawData(PC, Canvas); Canvas.Printf(TEXT(" ProjectField: %s"), *MyProjectState); } }; #endif Register your subclass instead of the stock one in your project's module startup. Performance CollectData is called once per tick per active category. Cost ≈ 10 µs (one GetActorOfClass + a few accessors + a perception query when an actor is selected). DrawData only runs when the HUD is visible, and it only draws text, so it costs very little. Shipping builds: no cost , because the whole category is compiled out by WITH_GAMEPLAY_DEBUGGER . Other LCM Nav3D debug tools r.LcmNav.Debug.StateTreeOverlay - on-screen pawn state DrawDebugString r.LcmNav.Debug.CoverViz - cover-spot DrawDebugSphere overlay r.LcmNav.Debug.FlowFieldViz - flow-field arrow grid LcmNavStress.SpawnAgents <N> - stress-spawn helper for scale testing

d: Navigate aquariums and other centimetre-scale volumes at a true 1 cm leaf, either at 100:1 or at 1:1 with the Small world-scale profile and scaled agents.
b: Documentation / Going Further / Small Worlds Tutorial 12 - Small worlds (centimetre-scale navigation) Applies to LCM Nav3D 3.6.0 · Unreal Engine 5.2 to 5.8 · Updated 22 November 2026 In short: the plugin voxelizes in Unreal units (1 uu = 1 cm). A 120 × 70 × 40 cm aquarium with 5 cm cave openings navigates at a 1 cm leaf with either of two setups: at 100:1 on any release, or at 1:1 with the World Scale profile set to Small . Both were tested in the same tank. Two rules to know first Set half the leaf you want. The octree halves a half-extent until it drops below Min Voxel Size , so the finest leaf lands at 2-4× the value. For a 1 cm leaf set 0.5. Make the world edge a power-of-two multiple of the leaf. World Extent is a cube half-extent centred on the world origin (the manager actor's location is ignored). With World Extent 64 and Min Voxel Size 0.5 the halving chain lands exactly on 1 cm; with 60 it lands on 0.94. Option A - build at 100:1 (works on every release) Setting Real In Unreal at 100:1 Tank 120 × 70 × 40 cm 12000 × 7000 × 4000 uu Manager: World Extent - 6400 (finite) Manager: Min Voxel Size - 50 Clearance Padding fish half-width half-width × 100 Fish speed 6 cm/s 600 uu/s (the shipped default) In testing, agents found and used a 5 cm cave mouth, a blocked cave was correctly reported as unreachable, and an agent crossed the tank in 3 s. Option B - build at 1:1 with World Scale = Small Set World Scale to Small , World Extent to 64, Min Voxel Size to 0.5. Clearance Padding is derived for you (half the leaf); the start-rescue distances and the large-node cost threshold scale with the leaf as well. The Details panel will tell you that the world is only 128 leaves across. That is normal for a small world. The line-of-sight sampler, the neighbour probe and the route executor's sampling floors follow the leaf on their own, on every profile. Agents follow too. The Fly To task (BT and StateTree) and the flight movement component carry an Agent Scale that defaults to 0 = follow the manager's World Scale, so under Small a fish authored with the shipped drone values (600 cm/s, 100 cm acceptance, 120 cm agent size) flies at 6 cm/s with a 1 cm acceptance and a 1.2 cm agent size, along the same path shape, in the same time. You still have to scale the pawn actor itself (mesh and collision) to match, because the plugin only scales the motion. Set Agent Scale explicitly on a task when an agent should not follow the world (a large creature in a small world, or the reverse). There is one engine limit for very small bodies. Unreal's swept movement pulls every blocking hit back by a fixed 0.1-1 cm, and it treats gaps inside the physics contact offset (2 cm minimum) as an overlap. So a body with collision of a centimetre or less touches walls differently from the same body at metre scale. We tested this with the bird pawn at agent scale 0.01. Its flight matched the 100:1 flight exactly until it first touched a wall (and in this tank it arrived sooner after that). Bodies that stay clear of walls, like the navigator drones, match exactly the whole way. If wall-hugging behaviour must match a metre-scale reference exactly, build at 10:1 (agent scale 0.1), where the engine tolerances are still small against the body. Stones with caves: use the collision The plugin decides what is solid from collision , not from the visible mesh. Set stone meshes to Use Complex Collision As Simple . A convex hull or box that covers a cave mouth makes the cave solid for the plugin, however small the leaf is. (In testing, the same tank with the stones' collision removed routed straight through them. With complex-as-simple collision the result was exactly the same as the reference.) Props that must not be solid Grass, backdrops and other dressing a body should pass through need the collision profile NoCollision , not only Collision Enabled = No Collision : a component that keeps the BlockAll profile gets its collision back when the map loads, and is then voxelized like stone. (In one test, seagrass saved that way blocked a 4 cm body from two of the demo tank's goals.) Mass crowds at small scale A Mass trait carries no reference-agent constants, so author its values in world centimetres: the demo school uses a 2 cm Agent Radius, 25 cm/s Max Speed and a 6 cm Arrive Radius. The flow field's own centimetre constants (the arrival stop, the goal cell, the obstacle skin and the slide's push cap) follow the World Scale automatically. The LCM Nav3D ISM Render trait has Mesh Rotation and Mesh Offset for a mesh not modelled facing +X; a fish modelled nose-along +Y needs Yaw -90. The demo tanks Demo/BehaviourTree/PreBaked_FiniteMaps/FishTank_BT , Demo/StateTree/.../FishTank_ST and Demo/MassEntity/.../FishTank_MassEntity are a 120 x 70 x 40 cm aquarium built this way (option B, a 1 cm leaf). Ten 8 cm fish on the Fish archetype roam through a rock arch and round a predator's lair their Prey filter prices x10; in the Mass tank a school of 40 follows a leader fish and parts round a predator that carries its own Territory. Your own aquarium: the checklist The demo tanks already have all of this set up. In your own tank, check each item. Agent Scale matches the fish. Every Flight Config value describes a ~1 m agent. Set the Flight Movement component's Agent Scale to the fish's length / 100 (0.08 for an 8 cm fish), and the same on its Fly To nodes - or set the navigation manager's World Scale instead. If you leave it at 1, an 8 cm fish swims at 280 cm/s like a metre-sized agent, with a turning circle of about 1.4 m. It then circles its targets and crashes into the rest of the school. The component says so in the Output Log, once per Blueprint, with the value to set. A Water Volume round the water. Add a Physics Volume , tick Water Volume , and size it to the water. A Fish-archetype body inside it never leaves it, and its top face is a navigation boundary, so routes stay under the surface. Without one, the plugin doesn't know where the water end

d: One Blueprint node that flies a pawn to a point or actor with no Behavior Tree, StateTree or AI Controller, with success, failure and cancel outputs.
b: Documentation / Going Further / Fly To Location Tutorial 13 - LCM Fly To Location (no Behavior Tree, no StateTree) Applies to LCM Nav3D 3.6.0 · Unreal Engine 5.2 to 5.8 · Updated 22 November 2026 In short: LCM Fly To Location is the flying counterpart of the engine's AI Move To node. Call it from any Blueprint - a level script, a pawn's Event Graph, a widget - with a pawn and a destination, and it fires On Success when the pawn arrives or On Fail with the reason it did not. The pawn needs no AI Controller, no Behavior Tree and no StateTree. What you need An LCM Nav3D Manager in the level, with navigation data built or baked (as for any agent). A pawn . Either kind works: With an enabled LCM Flight Movement Component , the pawn flies with its 6-DOF dynamics (banking, braking, a fish's tail), the same as it does under the Fly To tasks. The component's Agent Scale carries over, so a fish at 0.08 uses its own acceptance, speeds and clearances. Without one, the pawn is moved kinematically at Flight Speed . Using the node Right-click in a Blueprint graph and search for LCM Fly To Location (category LCM Nav3D | Movement ). Connect Pawn and Destination . Handle the two exec pins: On Success - the pawn has arrived. On Fail - it has not; the Result pin says why. Both pins also give Pawn Location , where the pawn was when the request ended. Input Default Meaning Pawn - The pawn to fly. Destination - Where to go. Ignored when Target Actor is set. Target Actor none Fly to this actor instead, re-planning as it moves. Acceptance Radius -1 Arrival distance in cm. <= 0 uses the Fly To default (100 cm, times the agent scale). Filter Class (advanced) none A navigation query filter: which cost areas this pawn avoids or prefers ( Tutorial 10 ). Chase Moving Target (advanced) off Aim where a moving Target Actor is going, not where it is. Flight Speed (advanced) -1 Kinematic pawns only: cruise speed in cm/s. <= 0 uses the default. Timeout Seconds (advanced) 0 Give up after this long. <= 0: no limit. Result Pin When Success On Success Arrived. No Path On Fail The destination cannot be reached from where the pawn is: sealed, outside the navigable volume, or excluded by the filter. Failed On Fail The pawn set off but could not complete the route. Aborted On Fail Cancelled, stopped, or replaced by a newer request for the same pawn. Timed Out On Fail Ran longer than Timeout Seconds. Invalid Request On Fail No pawn, or no LCM Nav3D Manager in the pawn's world. Fires at once. Stopping and replacing One request per pawn. A new LCM Fly To Location on a pawn that is already flying ends the old one with Aborted and takes over, as AI Move To does. Cancel (on the node's return value) or Stop LCM Fly To (on the pawn) ends the request with Aborted . Is LCM Fly To Active tells you whether a pawn is flying one. A stopped 6-DOF pawn holds where it was stopped instead of carrying on with its last command. A body that can't stop at once, like a fish or a bird, glides for its stopping distance and then comes back. With the demo fish, this was at most 4-7 cm past the point where it was cancelled, and it had settled within 2 cm of that point 4 s later. How arrival is judged A pawn arrives within Acceptance Radius of the destination. If the body reaches its last waypoint's neighbourhood and cannot close the final gap, it settles and completes within twice the radius. This is the Fly To tasks' rule. With a Target Actor , the pawn must reach the actor . With Chase Moving Target on, the pawn steers at a predicted intercept point, but reaching that point does not count as arriving; it keeps flying until it is within range of the actor itself. A path that is still being computed, or a streaming gap in an infinite world, is not a failure. The request waits. The request pauses with the game. It uses the same Fly To code The node has no movement code of its own. It runs the code of the StateTree Fly To task, with the same planner, cost areas, re-planning, streaming waits, avoidance, speed governor, arrival and hand-off to the flight component. A pawn flies the same way whether a tree or this node sends it. Do not drive one pawn from two places at once. A pawn running a Fly To task in a Behavior Tree or StateTree and an LCM Fly To Location at the same time has two sources of guidance; the last one each frame wins. Stop the tree's task (or leave the pawn without a tree) before using the node on it. From C++ #include "Agent/LCM_FlyToAsyncAction.h" ULcmFlyToLocationAsyncAction* Fly = ULcmFlyToLocationAsyncAction::FlyToLocation( this, MyPawn, FVector(4500, -2000, 800)); Fly->OnSuccess.AddDynamic(this, &AMyActor::HandleArrived); // UFUNCTION(ELcmFlyToResult, FVector) Fly->OnFail.AddDynamic(this, &AMyActor::HandleNotArrived); Fly->Activate(); In C++, bind the delegates before calling Activate() : an invalid request fires On Fail inside Activate() . The Blueprint node does this for you. How it is tested An automated test flies a pawn with no controller through the demo fish tank at a 1 cm leaf, and flies the stock navigator pawn across the metre-scale cost showcase. It covers every case on this page: an invalid request, arrival with a single On Success, never ending up inside rock or glass, No Path, replacing a request, Cancel and hold, and chasing a moving actor.

d: Make Unreal's own Move To, AI Move To and EQS plan through LCM Nav3D: supported agent setup, bridge states and how to check the proxy registered.
b: Documentation / Going Further / Stock Move To and EQS Tutorial 14 - Stock Move To and EQS with LCM Nav3D Applies to LCM Nav3D 3.6.0 · Unreal Engine 5.2 to 5.8 · Updated 22 November 2026 Goal: make UE's own navigation nodes ( Move To , AI Move To , Simple Move To , Find Path To Location Synchronously , EQS projection) plan through LCM Nav3D, and check that they do. How it works When a level has an LCM Nav3D Manager , the plugin spawns a navigation-data proxy ( LcmNavigationDataProxy ). It then asks UE's navigation system to register the proxy. Once registered, stock queries for the proxy's agent go through LCM Nav3D, and LCM Nav3D plans them in 3D. UE registers a navigation-data actor only for a Supported Agent whose Navigation Data Class is that actor's class. The plugin picks that agent for you where it can, and reports what really happened. (Before 3.4 the proxy was refused on every map while the log said "registered".) Step 1: pick your setup Your project What to do Only flying agents; no Recast navmesh in the level Nothing. The proxy claims the default agent on this world's navigation system ( r.LcmNav.Bridge.ClaimDefaultAgent 1 , the default). Project Settings are never written. Flying agents and ground characters on a Recast navmesh Add a Supported Agent for LCM Nav3D (Step 2). The navmesh keeps the default agent. You want the stock nodes to ignore LCM Nav3D r.LcmNav.Bridge.AutoRegister 0 . Step 2: add a Supported Agent (mixed projects only) Project Settings → Engine → Navigation System → Agents → Supported Agents → + . Name: anything, e.g. Flyer . Navigation Data Class: LcmNavigationDataProxy . Agent Radius / Height: your flyer's size. UE uses them to pick the agent for a pawn, so make them differ from the ground agent's. On the flying pawn's Character/Pawn Movement → Nav Agent Properties , use the same radius and height, or set Preferred Nav Data to LcmNavigationDataProxy . Step 3: check it worked The bridge reports one of these states, in the log and from Blueprint or C++ ( ULcmNavBridgeSubsystem::GetBridgeState() / GetBridgeStatusText() ): State Meaning Registered Stock queries for the bridged agent go through LCM Nav3D. NotClaimed Another navigation data (a Recast navmesh) owns the default agent, and no Supported Agent names the proxy. Do Step 2. Failed The navigation system refused the proxy. The status text gives UE's reason. Waiting / Requested Not settled yet (the navigation system registers on a later tick), or auto-registration is off. A warning appears once if the bridge ends in NotClaimed or Failed . It names the setting to change. Cost areas with the stock nodes A Filter Class on Move To (a NavigationQueryFilter ) works as it does with Recast. Its area costs and exclusions are applied by the LCM Nav3D planner, the same as on the LCM FlyTo nodes. Tutorial 10 covers cost-area volumes and filters. Limits The stock nodes follow the route with the pawn's own movement component. For 6-DOF flight dynamics (bank, thrust, archetypes), use the LCM Fly To BT or StateTree task, or the LCM Fly To Location Blueprint node. Move To path following in UE is ground-oriented: it projects points and treats acceptance in 2D unless the movement component flies. Give the pawn a flying movement mode, or use LCM Fly To.

d: Unreal Engine's stock Wait task works as-is with LCM Nav3D flying agents. The pattern, why no plugin variant ships, and the one LCM Nav3D-specific alternative.
b: Documentation / Behaviour Tree Patterns / Wait BT Wait - use stock UBTTask_Wait Applies to LCM Nav3D 3.6.0 · Unreal Engine 5.2 to 5.8 · Updated 22 November 2026 In short: Unreal Engine ships UBTTask_Wait . Use it. Pattern In your BT graph: right-click → Add Task → "Wait". Set WaitTime (seconds) + optional RandomDeviation . Task returns Succeeded after the timer. For a wait that depends on a blackboard-stored time, use UBTTask_WaitBlackboardTime instead. Why there is no LCM_BTTask_Wait It would do exactly the same thing as the stock task. The plugin has a StateTree version, FLcmSTTask_Wait , because StateTree on 5.2 has no stock Wait task. Behavior Trees have had one since UE 4, so an LCM Nav3D version would add nothing. LCM Nav3D-specific wait variant If you want to wait for a specific LCM Nav3D condition (e.g. "wait until the chunk at position X is loaded"), use the LCM Nav3D-unique: LCM_BTTask_ChunkPrewarm - waits for chunk readiness with a configurable timeout, proactively enqueues the chunk for generation

d: UBTDecorator_IsAtLocation already works on LCM Nav3D pawns. Three-step usage, why no plugin-specific variant exists, and when the path-finding variant helps.
b: Documentation / Behaviour Tree Patterns / Is At Location BT IsAtLocation - use the stock UE5 decorator Applies to LCM Nav3D 3.6.0 · Unreal Engine 5.2 to 5.8 · Updated 22 November 2026 In short: Unreal Engine already ships UBTDecorator_IsAtLocation . Use it directly on LCM Nav3D pawns. No LCM Nav3D-specific variant exists or is needed. Why there is no LCM_BTDecorator_IsAtLocation UBTDecorator_IsAtLocation already does everything an LCM Nav3D version would do: Reads a Vector or Object blackboard key Computes distance from the pawn to the key Returns true if within AcceptableRadius Optional bPathFindingBasedTest reuses the active path-following result This is the standard way to check "did the AI reach the location". A copy in LCM Nav3D would only make you choose between two identical nodes. Three-step usage on an LCM Nav3D pawn Drop the stock decorator on a Sequence / Selector node in your BT graph. Right-click → Add Decorator → "Is At Location". Set the blackboard key. Vector key (a goal position) or Object key (an AActor whose location is the goal - bUseNavAgentGoalLocation projects to nav-agent location). For LCM Nav3D flying pawns where you want the literal world position, use Vector. Set AcceptableRadius to your "we count this as arrived" distance in cm. Typical: 50-150 cm. The decorator works on every LCM Nav3D pawn that has an AIController, and you don't need any LCM Nav3D settings for it. When to use the path-finding variant UBTDecorator_IsAtLocation::bPathFindingBasedTest makes the decorator consistent with whatever was used to reach the location - useful when the move was via UBTTask_MoveTo (Recast) so the "arrived" check matches. For LCM Nav3D moves , this option will fall through to Recast even if your goal was inside an LCM Nav3D volume - leave it OFF and use straight geometric distance. Related LCM Nav3D-unique decorators For predicates that don't have a stock equivalent, see the LCM Nav3D-unique decorators we did ship: LCM_BTDecorator_PathLengthBelow - true-3D LCM Nav3D path-length check (stock DoesPathExist is binary + Recast) LCM_BTDecorator_HasLineOfSight - voxel-aware Lazy Theta* LOS (stock uses raycasts only) LCM_BTDecorator_IsInCover - composite SweepPenalty + LOS predicate LCM_BTDecorator_ChunkLoaded - SVO streaming probe LCM_BTDecorator_ThreatVisibleViaPerception - AIPerception + LCM Nav3D LOS composite These do things the stock nodes can't. "IsAtLocation" doesn't, so use the stock one.

d: When Unreal's stock Rotate to Face BB Entry task is right, why it misses targets above or below a flying agent, and when to use the LCM LookAt task.
b: Documentation / Behaviour Tree Patterns / Look At BT LookAt - choosing between the stock task and the LCM Nav3D one Applies to LCM Nav3D 3.6.0 · Unreal Engine 5.2 to 5.8 · Updated 22 November 2026 In short: Unreal Engine ships UBTTask_RotateToFaceBBEntry , and for a ground agent it is the right answer. For a flying agent it is not, because both its success test and its applied rotation ignore the vertical axis. LCM Nav3D now ships LCM_BTTask_LookAt and LCM_BTTask_TurnInPlace for that case. Which one to use Situation Use Ground agent, target roughly level with it Stock UBTTask_RotateToFaceBBEntry You want facing to persist across several tasks Stock task plus UBTService_DefaultFocus Target can be above or below the agent LCM_BTTask_LookAt You need a constant turn rate rather than an eased one LCM_BTTask_TurnInPlace You need the turn to hold position while it happens Either LCM task, with bHoldStation The stock task, and what it does with the vertical axis The stock task is well suited to walking agents and integrates with the AIController focus system, which is why it is the default recommendation in most UE projects. Two details matter once the agent can fly. Its success test is two dimensional. The task measures alignment with FVector::CosineAngle2D , which projects both directions onto the XY plane before comparing them. A target directly above the agent therefore has an angle difference of zero: the task reports success immediately, with the agent still pointing level. Its applied rotation drops pitch by default. The task rotates the pawn through the controller focus system, and APawn::FaceRotation keeps the pawn's existing pitch unless bUseControllerRotationPitch is set. On a default pawn that flag is false. Together those mean that, for a target overhead, the stock task can neither point the agent at it nor notice that it has not. None of this is a defect in the stock task. It is built for agents that move on a surface, where yaw is the only axis that matters. The LCM Nav3D tasks LCM_BTTask_LookAt eases toward the target; LCM_BTTask_TurnInPlace turns at a constant rate. They are otherwise the same node with a different rate mode, and both: measure the real 3D angle between the agent's forward vector and the target direction, so a pure pitch error reads as a pitch error; apply pitch as well as yaw; optionally hold position during the turn ( bHoldStation ), so a body with momentum does not drift while it rotates; optionally require line of sight, and wait rather than fail while navigation data is still streaming in. Property lists are in the API Reference . Pattern: face a target, then act Sequence LCM LookAt (TargetKey = ThreatActor) <your attack task> bFailOnTimeout defaults to false, so a turn that runs out of time still succeeds and the sequence continues. Set it true if a failed turn should abort the sequence. Pattern: keep facing while doing other things This is still the stock pattern and LCM Nav3D does not replace it: Add UBTService_DefaultFocus to the parent Selector or Sequence. Set its focus blackboard key. The controller holds focus for the whole subtree. Note: Do not run a focus service and a rotation task at the same time. The AIController re-asserts focus rotation every tick, so it will fight any task that writes rotation itself, including the LCM tasks. Pick one: a focus service for continuous facing, or a rotation task for a discrete turn. Running both has been observed to stall the agent outright. On 6-DOF flight bodies If the pawn carries LcmFlightMovementComponent with the flight dynamics locomotion model, that component owns the body's orientation and derives it from its own dynamics every tick. A rotation written by any task, stock or LCM, is overwritten in the same frame. The LCM tasks detect this and report the facing as unsupported rather than pretending to have turned; the task still succeeds so that a sequence containing it continues to work. Agents using the default kinematic locomotion model are unaffected and rotate normally. See also LCM_BTTask_MoveToAndFace - travel to a point and turn to face something on arrival, as one task. LCM_BTTask_Hover - hold position while facing a target, for a fixed time or indefinitely.

d: Turn a flying LCM Nav3D agent at a constant rate with the LCM TurnInPlace task, or keep facing a target across other tasks with the stock DefaultFocus service.
b: Documentation / Behaviour Tree Patterns / Turn In Place BT TurnInPlace - constant-rate turning, and the stock focus pattern Applies to LCM Nav3D 3.6.0 · Unreal Engine 5.2 to 5.8 · Updated 22 November 2026 In short: For continuous "keep facing while doing other things", use the stock UBTService_DefaultFocus . For a discrete turn at a constant rate, use LCM_BTTask_TurnInPlace , which ships with the plugin. See Look At for the full comparison between the stock rotation task and the LCM Nav3D ones. The short version: the stock task's success test projects onto the XY plane and its applied rotation drops pitch, so on a flying agent with a target overhead it can report success while still pointing level. Pattern: continuous facing during other tasks If you want the agent to keep facing a target while executing other tasks in a parent sequence, this is the stock pattern and LCM Nav3D does not replace it: Add UBTService_DefaultFocus to the parent Selector or Sequence. Set the focus blackboard key (Vector or Object). The AIController's focus stays set for the entire subtree, so the pawn faces the target through SetFocus while other tasks execute. This is the usual UE approach for combat AI that shoots while it strafes. Note: A focus service and a rotation task will fight each other. The controller re-asserts focus rotation every tick, overwriting anything a task writes, and this has been observed to stall an agent outright. Use a focus service for continuous facing or a rotation task for a discrete turn, not both on the same subtree. Pattern: a discrete constant-rate turn LCM_BTTask_TurnInPlace turns toward the target at MaxRotationRateDegPerSec and succeeds once it is pointing within AcceptableErrorDegrees . Sequence LCM TurnInPlace (TargetKey = ThreatActor, MaxRotationRateDegPerSec = 180) <your next task> Constant rate is the difference from LCM_BTTask_LookAt , which eases toward the target instead. Use the constant rate when the turn speed is a character trait you want to be visible and consistent, for instance a heavy gun platform that traverses slowly. Both tasks share the same underlying implementation and the same properties otherwise. bHoldStation defaults on, so the agent holds its position through the turn rather than drifting. Property list See the API Reference entry for LcmBTTask_TurnInPlace . On 6-DOF flight bodies Where LcmFlightMovementComponent is driving the pawn with the flight dynamics locomotion model, that component owns orientation and derives it from its own dynamics. The task reports the facing as unsupported rather than pretending, and still succeeds so surrounding sequences continue to work. Agents on the default kinematic locomotion model rotate normally.

d: Unreal ships all you need: a Float blackboard key plus a Blackboard-Compare decorator. The pattern, a GameplayTag variant, and why no LCM Nav3D node ships.
b: Documentation / Behaviour Tree Patterns / Health Below BT HealthBelow - use the stock blackboard + decorator pattern Applies to LCM Nav3D 3.6.0 · Unreal Engine 5.2 to 5.8 · Updated 22 November 2026 In short: Unreal Engine ships everything you need: a Float blackboard key + a Blackboard-Compare decorator. No LCM Nav3D variant. Pattern In your Blackboard asset : add a Float key CurrentHealth . In your AI controller / game code : write CurrentHealth whenever damage is applied. In your BT graph : add a Blackboard decorator to the "retreat" / "panic" sequence. Set: Key: CurrentHealth Notify Observer: On Value Change (so the decorator re-evaluates immediately on damage) Operator: Is Less Than Value: 30.0 (or whatever threshold) This is the usual UE5 way to do "if health is below X, do Y". If you want a GameplayTag-based pattern For projects using GAS where health states are tags (e.g. Status.Bleeding , Status.LowHealth ), use the stock UBTDecorator_CheckGameplayTagsOnActor . Same semantics, tag-driven. Why there is no LCM_BTDecorator_HealthBelow The stock blackboard-compare decorator does the same job, with one extra dropdown for the comparison operator. That gives you more options ( > < <= >= == ) than a fixed "below threshold" LCM Nav3D decorator. Use the stock decorator. The StateTree version, FLcmSTCondition_HealthBelow , is still included so it is easy to find in the StateTree node picker. It also just compares two floats, the same as the stock decorator. Related LCM Nav3D-unique decorators If your "should I retreat" gate isn't health-based but threat-field-based , these LCM Nav3D nodes are a better fit: LCM_BTDecorator_IsInCover - composite SweepPenalty + LOS predicate LCM_BTService_ThreatFieldSampler - writes CurrentThreatLevel + bInThreatZone into BB every 0.2s; then a stock blackboard decorator can gate on bInThreatZone

d: UAIPerceptionComponent already emits perception updates as a delegate. Bind it in your AI controller and write to a blackboard key - no custom BT service needed.
b: Documentation / Behaviour Tree Patterns / Perception Relay BT PerceptionRelay - bind OnTargetPerceptionUpdated directly Applies to LCM Nav3D 3.6.0 · Unreal Engine 5.2 to 5.8 · Updated 22 November 2026 In short: Unreal Engine's UAIPerceptionComponent already emits perception updates as a delegate. You don't need a custom BT service - just bind the delegate in your AI controller and write to a blackboard key. Pattern (in your AIController subclass) // In your AIController.h UPROPERTY() TObjectPtr<UAIPerceptionComponent> PerceptionComp; UFUNCTION() void OnPerceptionUpdate(AActor* Actor, FAIStimulus Stimulus); // In your AIController.cpp BeginPlay PerceptionComp = FindComponentByClass<UAIPerceptionComponent>(); if (PerceptionComp) { PerceptionComp->OnTargetPerceptionUpdated.AddDynamic( this, &AYourAIController::OnPerceptionUpdate); } void AYourAIController::OnPerceptionUpdate(AActor* Actor, FAIStimulus Stimulus) { if (UBlackboardComponent* BB = GetBlackboardComponent()) { if (Stimulus.WasSuccessfullySensed()) { BB->SetValueAsObject("ClosestThreat", Actor); BB->SetValueAsBool ("bHasAnyTarget", true); } else { // Lost sight - leave ClosestThreat for memory pattern (see below) BB->SetValueAsBool("bHasAnyTarget", false); } } } This is the usual UE5 approach: three lines in your AIController and a Blackboard decorator in the BT. Why there is no LCM_BTService_PerceptionRelay A custom service that ticks each frame and re-queries GetCurrentlyPerceivedActors is less efficient than binding the event-driven OnTargetPerceptionUpdated delegate. It is also the approach most UE5 AI tutorials use, so it will look familiar. The LCM Nav3D StateTree variant FLcmSTEval_PerceptionRelay is kept because StateTree has no per-state perception delegate (its evaluators are tick-based by design). On the BT side, delegate binding is the standard. Memory pattern (last-known-location with age) UE5's perception component already tracks last-known location + age per perceived actor via FActorPerceptionInfo::GetLastStimulusLocation(float* OutAge) . To use it: if (const FActorPerceptionInfo* Info = PerceptionComp->GetActorInfo(*Actor)) { float Age = 0.f; FVector LastKnown = Info->GetLastStimulusLocation(&Age); if (Age < 8.f) // 8 sec memory window { BB->SetValueAsVector("LastKnownThreatLoc", LastKnown); } } See BT_MemoryDecay_StockPattern.md for the full pattern. Don't roll your own decay timer - perception's age tracking already does it for you. Related LCM Nav3D-unique services For perception-aware predicates that need LCM Nav3D LOS (volumetric, not raycast): LCM_BTDecorator_ThreatVisibleViaPerception - composite: perception sees + LCM Nav3D Lazy Theta* LOS is clear LCM_BTService_SquadSnapshot - aggregates perceived allies into squad centroid / cohesion radius

d: Unreal's UAIPerceptionComponent already tracks per-actor last-known stimulus location with age. Use it as a BT service instead of a hand-rolled decay timer.
b: Documentation / Behaviour Tree Patterns / Memory Decay BT MemoryDecay - use FActorPerceptionInfo::GetLastStimulusLocation(&OutAge) Applies to LCM Nav3D 3.6.0 · Unreal Engine 5.2 to 5.8 · Updated 22 November 2026 In short: Unreal Engine's UAIPerceptionComponent already tracks per-actor last-known stimulus location with age. No need to roll your own decay timer. Pattern (in your AIController or a small custom service) UAIPerceptionComponent* Perception = GetAIPerceptionComponent(); if (!Perception) return; // Pull the last-known info for a specific actor (e.g. the threat you're tracking). if (const FActorPerceptionInfo* Info = Perception->GetActorInfo(*ThreatActor)) { float Age = 0.0f; FVector LastKnown = Info->GetLastStimulusLocation(&Age); // Apply your project's memory window. if (Age < MemoryWindowSec) { Blackboard->SetValueAsVector("LastKnownThreatLoc", LastKnown); Blackboard->SetValueAsFloat ("MemoryAge", Age); Blackboard->SetValueAsBool ("bHasMemory", true); } else { // Memory expired. Blackboard->SetValueAsBool("bHasMemory", false); } } The perception component tracks the age for you. It resets the age on each new stimulus and increases it every frame. How to integrate as a BT service Wrap the snippet above in a UBTService_BlueprintBase subclass (Blueprint-only - no C++ needed): Create a BP service. Override Receive Tick . Inputs: ThreatActor (Object BB key) + MemoryWindowSec (float). Inputs to write: LastKnownThreatLoc (Vector BB key) + MemoryAge (Float BB key) + bHasMemory (Bool BB key). Tick body: get perception component → GetActorInfo → GetLastStimulusLocation(&Age) → branch on Age vs window → write BB keys. Five nodes total. No C++ required. Why there is no LCM_BTService_MemoryDecay The stock FActorPerceptionInfo::GetLastStimulusLocation(&OutAge) already gives you everything a MemoryDecay service would. It tracks location and age per sense and per actor , resets on each stimulus and ages every frame. A separate decay timer in the plugin would: Duplicate the perception component's bookkeeping Miss the per-sense granularity (perception tracks separately for Sight / Hearing / Damage / etc.) Force you to maintain two parallel "last seen" caches In StateTree, you can use the plugin's FLcmSTEval_Memory evaluator. Related LCM Nav3D-unique services If you want squad-level memory (where multiple allies' perceived-actor lists are aggregated), use LCM_BTService_SquadSnapshot . The stock nodes have nothing like it.

d: Ready-made flying-agent behaviours for Behavior Tree, StateTree and Mass: Engage, Investigate, Flee, Scan Area, Perch, Land and Take Off, with their settings.
b: Behaviour Nodes: Engage, Investigate, Flee, Scan Area, Perch Applies to LCM Nav3D 3.6.0 · Unreal Engine 5.2 to 5.8 · Updated 22 November 2026 LCM Nav3D ships ready-made behaviours for flying and swimming agents. Each one plans its own 3D route, moves the body through its Flight Movement component, and ends with Succeeded or Failed. That way you can build an agent's behaviour by putting nodes together instead of writing movement code. Behaviour What the agent does Ends with Engage Target Picks a firing position with a clear line of sight inside the weapon's range and gimbal limits, flies there, keeps the target in view as it moves, and sets Fire Allowed while a shot is good. Succeeded when its engagement window (Max Duration) ends. Failed when it loses the target and a short search at its last-known position does not find it, or no firing position can be reached. Investigate Flies to a vantage point with a clear view of a last-known position, looks round, then searches on along the way the target was heading. Succeeded when it sees the target or finishes the search (Failed instead with Fail If Not Found). Flee Gets away from a threat to cover: a point far from it, not toward it, that it cannot see into. Keeps re-checking as the threat moves. Succeeded once hidden and unseen for Hide Seconds . Scan Area Sweeps a volume from a set of viewpoints, turning round at each, until the whole volume has been seen. Succeeded when the volume is covered, or early when the watched-for actor is seen. Perch Lands on the nearest reachable surface tagged as a perch (rack tops, beams, ledges, pads). Succeeded once down; Failed when no perch is reachable. Land / Take Off Touch down on a site (including a moving deck or a site under a roof) and climb away again, each archetype in its own way: drones descend vertically, birds and fish glide in with a flare. Succeeded once down / once at height. Three editions of every node Behavior Tree tasks, in the task list under their own names (Engage Target, Investigate, Flee, Scan Area, Perch, Land, Take Off). StateTree tasks, under LCM Nav3D , for pawns driven by a StateTree component. Mass crowd tasks, under LCM Nav3D (Engage (Group), Investigate (Crowd), Scan Area (Crowd), Flee, Perch), for Mass StateTrees. The settings are the same in all three, so the reference below only lists them once. Agents share the work Agents on the same world never take the same perch, the same cover or the same firing position or viewpoint: each claim lives while its agent is heading for it or holding it. Pawns and Mass entities share one set of claims, so a flock of Mass birds and a pawn bird spread over the ledges together. Wiring Engage and Investigate to AI Perception Give the pawn an AI Perception component with a sight sense, and make the target perceivable. Add the LCM Perceived Actor To Blackboard service to the branch. Set Result Key (Object) and, for Investigate, Last Known Location Key and Last Known Velocity Key (Vectors). Put Engage Target under a decorator on the Result Key with Observer Aborts: Lower Priority , and Investigate below it, reading the last-known keys. When the target is lost, Investigate searches where it went; when it is seen again, Engage takes over. Perches and landing sites Tag the surfaces agents may land on (an actor tag or a component tag, Perch by default) and set the Perch node's Perch Tag . For your own site selection, the EQS generator LCM Nav3D | Landing Sites and the test LCM Nav3D | Landable find flat, clear, reachable touchdown points for a flying agent; feed the best one to Land. Demo levels to study Every behaviour runs in the LCM Nav3D Samples demo levels (the free LCM Nav3D Samples download; see Installation): Hunter Drone (Engage), Harbour (Land on moving surfaces), Sea Cliffs (Perch, Flee, Take Off), Coral Reef (fish: Flee, Perch), Warehouse (Scan Area, Engage, Investigate, Flee, Perch) and Sentry Drones (perception, EQS firing positions, landing under cover), each in Behavior Tree, StateTree and Mass editions. Reference Engage Target Settings ( LcmBTTask_EngageTarget ) TargetKey - The actor to engage. FireAllowedKey - Optional (Bool): true while a shot is good. Drive the weapon task's decorator with it. AimPointKey - Optional (Vector): where to shoot - leads the target by the projectile's flight time. Position - Where to take position (range and altitude bands, weights). Route - How the route there is flown. Tracking - How the target is tracked. Sighting - Where sightings come from: the node's own line of sight, or the AI Perception sight sense. TargetWalks - The target walks (a character): predictions stop at walls and follow the ground. Off for a flyer. TargetRadiusCm - Body radius of the target, for the walker prediction. MaxSightRangeCm - Farthest the agent can see the target from. PositionLeadSeconds - Choose the firing position around where the target will be this far ahead. FiringPositionQuery - Optional: an EQS query chooses the firing position instead of the built-in rings (querier = the pawn). Use the "LCM Nav3D | Engaged Target" / "Engaged Target (Predicted)" contexts to build it around the target. Asked every RechooseIntervalSeconds; when it finds nothing the built-in choice is used for that interval. RechooseIntervalSeconds - Re-choose the firing position this often (seconds). ProjectileSpeedCmS - Projectile speed for aim lead (cm/s). 0 = hitscan: aim at the target itself. AimToleranceDegrees - The envelope: aim error, range band, and how long it must hold before firing is allowed. GimbalMinPitchDegrees - The weapon sits on a GIMBAL that pitches independently of the body - a multirotor can only yaw its body, and a drone above a walking target must aim DOWN. The envelope therefore checks the body's YAW error against AimToleranceDegrees and the PITCH the shot needs against these limits (degrees, negative = down). d: Eight walk-through levels in the style of Epic's Content Examples: 69 single-feature displays that check themselves as they run and name the chapter to read.
b: Feature Examples Applies to LCM Nav3D 3.6.0 · Unreal Engine 5.2 to 5.8 · Updated 22 November 2026 Eight levels in the style of Epic's Content Examples: every display shows one feature of LCM Nav3D working, with a plaque that says what to look at and which chapter to read. They come with the free LCM Nav3D Samples download ( LCM Nav3D menu → Get the Demo Levels (free)... ), under Content/Showcase/ ; the demo menu lists them under Feature Examples . The tables below are written out from the levels themselves, so they match what is in each level. Using a level Walk with W A S D and the mouse. A display starts when you walk up to it and resets when you leave. Tab / Shift+Tab jump to the next / previous display. R replays the one you are at. O switches the planned routes on and off (the Navigation Manager's Draw Flight Paths). H hides the HUD; Esc returns to the demo menu. Each display checks itself : its lines on the HUD turn PASS (green) or FAIL (red) as the demo runs. Every tree, query and crowd config a display uses sits in Showcase/SC_0N/DN_M/ , named for what it does - open it to see how the display is built. 1. Navigation Basics /LCMNav3DSamples/Showcase/SC_01_NavigationBasics - 7 displays. What 3D navigation is before any behaviour: one manager, an octree of free space, paths through it. Walk up to a display to start it. O shows the planned routes; Tab jumps to the next display. # Display What it shows Read 1.1 The Navigation Manager One LCM Navigation Manager covers this level with an octree of the free space, padded by the agents' size. Tutorial 02, The one actor you must place 1.2 Agent size Both drones fly to the far side of the wall. The blue one fits through the window. Settings Reference, Per-agent settings 1.3 Path smoothing The same hop over a crate, planned two ways. Back lane: Raw Path, the solver's straight segments. Troubleshooting, No path found 2. Flight and Locomotion /LCMNav3DSamples/Showcase/SC_02_FlightLocomotion - 8 displays. The bodies the navigation flies: drone, jet, bird and fish, each with its own 6-DOF dynamics. They use the same nodes and the same paths, but each body has different physics. Tab jumps to the next display. # Display What it shows Read 2.1 Four flight archetypes A drone, a jet, a bird and a fish fly the same kind of loop, each in its own lane. Flight Locomotion Reference, Archetypes 2.2 Kinematic and Flight Dynamics Two drones, the same Fly To, the same path. Left: Locomotion Model Kinematic - the body follows the line. Flight Locomotion Reference, Guidance 2.3 Tuning: agile and gentle Two drones on the same course. Agile: Max Tilt 60, Max Acceleration 2000. Gentle: 20 and 500. Flight Locomotion Reference, Winged bodies 2.5 Bird: flight and a perched landing A gull flaps to climb and glides to cruise. LCM Perch brings it in on a braking flare onto the ledge.
